A solar eclipse belongs to the EARTH marker: it relocates to the ring band, swaps its face for the black eclipsed-Sun plate, and lights a glow whose colour and strength name the kind — as the four chapters that follow describe. If the shadow's path runs far from your city, or the Sun has already set, the glow mutes to a quiet silver and the hover tells you why: the eclipse is real, but not yours to see from here.

Solar_Total.title: Total Solar Eclipse
Solar_Total.base:
[[The Sky]] In a total solar eclipse the Moon covers the Sun's disc exactly — a coincidence of scale the sky owes to arithmetic, the Sun about four hundred times wider than the Moon and about four hundred times farther away, so the two appear the same size. For a few minutes the umbra sweeps a narrow path across the Earth at over a thousand kilometres an hour, and inside that path the day goes dark.

[[What You See]] Totality is unlike anything else in the sky. The temperature drops, bright stars come out at noon, and around the black disc the Sun's pearl-white CORONA — its million-degree outer atmosphere, invisible at any other time — stands open to the naked eye. A ruby bead of the chromosphere flashes at the rim as the last light goes and again as it returns. This is the only moment it is ever safe to look at the Sun unfiltered, and only during totality itself.

[[On the Dial]] The Earth marker wears the black eclipsed-Sun plate and its glow burns at FULL strength — the corona drawn as light rather than as a picture, exactly as our canon promised: no new art, the halo does the work. Total is the strongest state the dial knows.

[[How Often]] Somewhere on Earth roughly once every eighteen months; over any single town, on average about once in 375 years.

[[The Anchor]] Herodotus tells of the eclipse of 585 BCE that stopped a battle: the Medes and Lydians, five years at war, saw "the day turned suddenly to night," took it for a sign, and made peace on the spot. Thales of Miletus was said to have foretold it — the first eclipse in recorded history a philosopher claimed to predict.

Solar_Annular.title: Annular Solar Eclipse
Solar_Annular.base:
[[The Sky]] An annular eclipse is a total eclipse that falls short. The alignment is perfect, but the Moon is near apogee, the far point of its slightly oval orbit, where it looks a shade too small to cover the Sun. The umbra's tip stops short of the ground; only its continuation past that point, the antumbra, reaches you.

[[What You See]] The Moon slides dead-centre over the Sun and leaves a brilliant, unbroken RING of sunlight around itself — the ring of fire. The sky dims but never falls to night, no corona appears, and it is NEVER safe to look without a proper filter: a blinding sliver of the Sun's surface is showing the entire time.

[[On the Dial]] Annular shares the black-sun plate with total, but its glow burns in its OWN hotter orange-red — the ring of fire given its own colour, at full strength — so the two states that look most alike in the sky never read the same on the dial.

[[How Often]] Slightly more common than total eclipses: the Moon spends a little more of its orbit far from Earth than near it, so a few fall each decade worldwide.

[[The Anchor]] Early astronomers puzzled long over how the very same geometry could hide the Sun completely one year and leave a bright ring the next. The answer — the Moon's own changing distance along its ellipse — was one of the clean confirmations that the lunar orbit is not a circle but an oval, exactly as Kepler's laws require.

Solar_Partial.title: Partial Solar Eclipse
Solar_Partial.base:
[[The Sky]] Every total and annular eclipse is partial for the wide regions on either side of its central path, and some eclipses are partial for everyone — the umbra misses the Earth entirely, sailing above a pole, and only the penumbra ever touches the surface.

[[What You See]] The Moon takes a curved bite out of the Sun and no more. The light dims a little if the bite is deep, shadows sharpen, and pinholes — the gaps between leaves, the holes in a colander — cast tiny crescent suns across the ground. It is never safe to view unfiltered; no part of the Sun is ever covered enough.

[[On the Dial]] Partial is the one solar state whose glow still scales with MAGNITUDE — how much of the Sun is hidden. A shallow bite glows faintly, a deep one strongly, tracking the number the hover reads out. It keeps the same black-sun plate as the others.

[[How Often]] The most frequently SEEN kind, precisely because its reach is widest — most people's "I once saw an eclipse" was a partial one, watched from just off some total eclipse's path.

[[The Anchor]] It was a TOTAL eclipse, on 29 May 1919, that let Eddington measure starlight bending around the Sun and confirmed Einstein overnight — but seen from anywhere off its narrow track, that same event was only a partial. The quiet majority of partials are the frame around every famous total one.

Solar_Hybrid.title: Hybrid Solar Eclipse
Solar_Hybrid.base:
[[The Sky]] A hybrid eclipse is the rarest kind, the knife-edge between total and annular. Along the middle of its track the umbra just reaches the ground and the eclipse is total; toward the ends, where the Earth curves away and adds a few thousand kilometres of distance, the same shadow falls short and the same eclipse turns annular. The curvature of the planet alone decides which you get.

[[What You See]] Observers near the centre of the path see totality, with its corona; observers near the beginning and end of the very same event see a ring of fire. One eclipse, two faces, sorted purely by where you stand on the curve of the Earth.

[[On the Dial]] Because a hybrid shows true totality along most of its ground track, the dial renders it as its stronger face — the same black-sun plate and full glow as a TOTAL eclipse — while keeping its own chapter and emblem here so the reader knows the difference. It is the closer of the two sealed states, chosen on purpose, never the unknown-type fallback.

[[How Often]] Only a few percent of all solar eclipses are hybrid — a small handful each century.

[[The Anchor]] The hybrid eclipse of 3 November 2013 began annular at sunrise over the western Atlantic and ended total over central Africa — a single shadow changing its mind across an ocean, exactly as the geometry demands.

Lunar_Overview.title: Lunar Eclipses
Lunar_Overview.base:
[[The Sky]] A lunar eclipse happens only at Full Moon, when the Earth stands between the Sun and the Moon and casts its own shadow across the Moon's face. Like solar eclipses they fall only near a node, so not every Full Moon qualifies. But a lunar eclipse is visible from the ENTIRE night side of the Earth at once — half the planet watches the same darkening at the same moment — which is why any given place sees far more lunar eclipses than total solar ones.

[[The Three Kinds]] Earth's shadow has two parts. The dark central umbra, where the Sun is fully blocked, gives a TOTAL eclipse when the whole Moon is inside it and a PARTIAL eclipse when only part of the Moon enters. The faint outer penumbra, where the Sun is merely partly blocked, gives a PENUMBRAL eclipse — a subtle shading most people would never notice.

[[On the Dial]] A lunar eclipse belongs to the MOON marker. Unlike a solar eclipse, its whole signature is a true DARKENING of the disc — the brightness turned down, never a translucent wash a bright pixel can bleed through — set by the kind, plus a bronze glow and, for the deeper kinds, a thin turquoise fringe at the shadow's rim. The three chapters that follow read straight off the dial's own state table.

Lunar_Total.title: Total Lunar Eclipse
Lunar_Total.base:
[[The Sky]] In a total lunar eclipse the whole Moon passes into Earth's dark umbra. Yet it does not vanish. Earth's atmosphere bends and filters sunlight around the planet's rim and throws it inward onto the Moon, and because that light has been reddened — every sunrise and sunset happening on Earth at once, projected onto the lunar face — the eclipsed Moon glows a deep coppery red.

[[What You See]] The BLOOD MOON: a dim, ruddy disc whose exact shade is set by how much dust and cloud ring the Earth that night. A thin band of turquoise sometimes edges the shadow at the start and end — sunlight filtered through the ozone layer high up rather than the lower air, the one part of the atmosphere that lets blue through.

[[On the Dial]] Total is the dial's darkest lunar state: the disc drops to about seven percent brightness AND takes a deep copper tint, so it reads dark and unmistakably red rather than flat grey. The bronze glow burns at full strength and wears the turquoise ozone fringe at its outer edge — the state table's most complete picture. Only totality dims the whole face enough for the colour cast to read honestly.

[[How Often]] Roughly one total lunar eclipse a year on average, and visible to anyone on the night side — most people have seen several without travelling at all.

[[The Anchor]] Columbus, stranded in Jamaica in 1504, used an almanac's prediction of a total lunar eclipse to frighten the islanders into feeding his crew: he "took the Moon away," gave it back blood-red, then restored it on schedule. The blood moon has meant omen and portent in nearly every culture that ever watched the sky — and it is our own canon's NINTH MOOD, the Eclipse.

Lunar_Partial.title: Partial Lunar Eclipse
Lunar_Partial.base:
[[The Sky]] A partial lunar eclipse is one where only part of the Moon crosses into the umbra. The alignment near the node is close but not exact, so Earth's dark shadow covers a fraction of the disc while the rest sits in the softer penumbra.

[[What You See]] A clean, curved bite taken out of the Full Moon, the umbra's edge visibly round — one of the oldest proofs that the Earth is a sphere, since only a ball casts a round shadow from every angle. The covered part often glows faintly red like a total eclipse; the uncovered part stays bright.

[[On the Dial]] The dial darkens the whole disc to about eighteen percent of full brightness — clearly dimmed, but not the near-black of totality — in plain neutral grey, with a bronze glow at reduced strength and the turquoise fringe still shown. One measured step down from total on every axis.

[[How Often]] About as common as total lunar eclipses, a little more so, since a wider spread of near-node alignments produces one.

[[The Anchor]] Aristotle argued from exactly this shadow, in the fourth century BCE, that the Earth must be a sphere: the edge of its shadow on the Moon is always the arc of a circle, whatever the Moon's height in the sky — a partial eclipse doing the reasoning for him.

Lunar_Penumbral.title: Penumbral Lunar Eclipse
Lunar_Penumbral.base:
[[The Sky]] A penumbral eclipse is the faintest of all. The Moon misses Earth's dark umbra entirely and passes only through the penumbra, the outer shadow where the Sun is merely partly blocked. No part of the Moon is ever in full shadow.

[[What You See]] Almost nothing. One edge of the Full Moon dims very slightly, as though a thin veil had been drawn across it — so subtle that a casual glance misses it and only a careful eye or a photograph catches the shading at all. There is no bite, no red, no drama.

[[On the Dial]] The dial is honest about this: the disc dims only to about sixty percent brightness — still plainly a Moon — in neutral grey, the bronze glow is at its weakest, and there is NO turquoise fringe, because a real penumbral eclipse shows no such rim. The gentlest state the table holds.

[[How Often]] Common, but the least remarked — many pass entirely unnoticed even by people looking straight at the Moon.

[[The Anchor]] Penumbral eclipses rarely reached the history books precisely because they are so faint; the old records that mention a Full Moon "dimmed" or "sickly" with no bite taken out of it are the closest the ancient sky-watchers came to noting one — the eclipse that hides even while it happens.

Lucifer.base:
[[The Story]] Lucifer is the morning star — in the old readings the most beautiful of the lights, the bearer of the dawn — who looked at his own shining and ruled it should be worshiped. 'I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High': the one recorded ambition is not to destroy the throne but to sit on it. He is the far end of love of self — pride grown past every correction — and his fall is its oldest measure: like lightning, from heaven, downward.

[[On the Dial]] His sign is the rising triangle — the Flame the ring already carries: fire climbing to a point, aimed at the top of the dial where the crown of noon sits. His color is red, the pigment world's peak — the last intensification light passes through before it turns on itself. On the dial's own Sunday the ruler face carries exactly his vice: Pride, the crown forgetting it is worn on behalf of the whole week.

[[The Sky]] The sky offers a precise image of him. A star can die in two directions, and his is the explosion: the supernova — the star that burns everything it has in one climb, briefly outshining every other light in the sky, exactly as it destroys itself. That is pride's whole arc drawn in physics: the blaze upward, aimed at the top of the dial where noon sits, magnificent for a moment and gone.

[[The Lesson]] On the scale of self he stands at the right-hand extreme — plus infinity, red. What he never had was his antidote: the falling triangle across the beam. Nothing weighed on the other pan, and a scale with one loaded pan is not a scale; it is a fall already in progress.

Judas.base:
[[The Story]] Judas Iscariot kept the purse of the twelve and sold the one he followed for thirty pieces of silver, marking him with a kiss so the torches would take the right man. But the act that sets him at the extreme is not the betrayal — it is the verdict he passed afterward, on himself. He judged Judas unforgivable, and carried out the sentence with his own hands. He is the far end of hatred of self: the servant who rules that he is worth nothing.

[[On the Dial]] His sign is the falling triangle — the Chalice: water pouring to a point, aimed at the dial's midnight. His color is blue, the first color darkness makes, the hue of retreat and of cold. And the sky's image of him is the star's OTHER death: the collapse inward — the star that falls into itself until not even its own light is allowed to leave. The black hole sits where his triangle points, at the bottom of the 24-hour dial: midnight, the swallowed light. On the dial's Sunday the servant face carries exactly his vice: service curdled into self-erasure.

[[The Story]] The same night measures him against his own antidote. Peter failed too — three denials before the rooster crowed — and wept, and came back, and was handed the keys. The difference between the two failures is one decision: Peter let himself be forgiven; Judas ruled that mercy could not reach his case. That ruling is pride's mirror image — deciding your own verdict outranks everyone else's, including the one you betrayed. And the pattern is older than him: Ahithophel, David's wisest counselor, betrayed his king and hanged himself when the plot soured.

[[The Lesson]] On the scale of self he stands at the left-hand extreme — minus infinity, blue. His antidote existed — it had washed his feet that same evening — and he never took it. The falling triangle, alone, falls.

The Union.base:
[[The Figure]] Every person lives somewhere on the beam between the two triangles — loving themselves enough to stand and be defended, doubting themselves enough to be corrected. The two names mark the ends no one should reach, and the fight they define is not a fight between two men: it runs inside one. The man who at once loves and hates himself reads himself from both ends — the love keeps him from being trampled, the hate keeps him honest — and between the two readings he walks upright.

The zero of that scale is reached by no individual: the extremes themselves prove it, two weights that dropped off the pendulum because each swung with nothing on the other side. They never had each other — Lucifer with no falling triangle to doubt him, Judas with no rising one to defend him — so each is the other's missing antidote. Together they would see everything, from both absolute ends at once; and that seat belongs to no one alone.

[[On the Dial]] The dial answers with geometry. Lay the falling triangle over the rising one and the instrument's own star appears — the hexagram: Flame over Chalice, red over blue, the Seal the ring's letters already wear. That is why Sunday, alone of the days, has two faces: a ruler who must not become Lucifer and a servant who must not become Judas, sharing one seat so that neither pole is ever left alone with itself. And between the star's two deaths — the explosion upward and the collapse inward — stands the star that does neither: the Sun, which simply gives its light away, steadily, every day. The white center — Glory, the sum of every color — sits exactly where the two triangles cross.

[[The Lesson]] And if the scale needs a figure standing at its zero, he is not at Judas's end. The one who allowed his own death did not do it out of hatred of self: he gave himself away while never once denying who he was — king and servant in one person, washing feet with the same hands that carry the scepter. Permitting your own execution out of love is the gift of a whole self, not the disposal of a worthless one; that is the zero embodied, the union the two extremes never made. The minus end keeps its own name: the man who decided mercy could not reach him.

Sigma.base:
[[The Ninth]] Seven ranked wolves plus Sunday's Alpha-Omega pair fill the Wolf Pack's eight regular seats, one name for what a pack needs at each life stage, all the way down to the servant Omega the ring's own midnight letter already spells. Sigma is the ninth, and unlike every other ninth in this encyclopedia it never came from the science it borrows its name from. The whole alpha-to-omega ladder was drawn up from wolves crowded into captivity in the 1940s; L. David Mech, the researcher who coined "alpha," spent decades afterward trying to retract the term once he learned that real wild packs are just families, no ladder anyone climbs. "Sigma" was invented online long after, for a wolf that opts out of ranking entirely — ethology's ghost, not its opposite pole.

[[The Lesson]] No duality is asked of Sigma here, and rightly so: the owner's own note is that it stands equal in stature to the Alpha rather than opposite it, a wolf outside the hierarchy rather than its counterweight. Forcing it onto either end of the Lucifer-Judas scale would invent an opposition the wolf itself never claimed.

The eight ranks below it all answer to a mate, a den, a pup, a pace — real needs of a real pack. Sigma is the seat that reminds the other eight that not every name carved onto this dial was found in the wild; some were only ever a story a species told about itself.

The Swarm.base:
[[The Ninth]] Queen and Cleaner share Sunday's two faces, and six working castes — Forager, Drone and the rest — fill the days between them, each one an office a bee is born or raised into inside the hive's own temporal polyethism. The Swarm is the ninth, and it holds no office at all: it is the one event the entire colony performs together, the moment the whole structure gets up and leaves. When a hive outgrows itself, the old queen and roughly half the workers abandon a comb that could still make honey and fly off as a single body to found a nest from nothing — one of the best-documented behaviors in apiculture, and still the strangest to watch: a building deciding to become a cloud.

[[The Lesson]] The sheet asks for no axis here, and honestly: the Swarm is not the hive's extreme of pride or self-erasure, not a caste pushed to a pole. It stands beside the Queen and the Cleaner as a happening rather than a rank, so no reading from the Lucifer-Judas scale has anywhere true to land.

The six castes each keep the hive alive by staying exactly at their post. The Swarm is there to remind them the hive was never the comb, the wax, or the walls — it was always the bees, and the day they choose to leave, they carry the whole colony with them and lose nothing that mattered.

The Graveyard.base:
[[The Ninth]] A living Matriarch and her Sunday-servant twin, Memory, hold the two faces of the day the Elephant Herd's whole claim on a clock rests on; six more elephants fill the week around them, each one remembered as an individual by the herd that outlives it. The Graveyard is the ninth, and it carries that same memory one step further than any single elephant can — past the animal that remembers, into the place where remembering hardens into a story outsiders tell. The "elephant graveyard," a hidden valley every elephant supposedly seeks out alone to die in, has no support in the actual science; real herds do linger over a dead kin's bones and show something close to grief, but no chosen dying-ground has ever been found. The legend almost certainly grew out of ivory-hunters' tales, not out of anything elephants do.

[[The Lesson]] No duality is claimed for the Graveyard, and the sheet is plain about why: an animal society was never built on the self-love-versus-self-hate axis the Lucifer-Judas scale measures, so no reading from it has honest footing here.

The herd remembers one death at a time, by scent, by name, by the exact weight of a particular bone. The Graveyard is what happens after — when private grief gets retold so many times by people who never knew the dead that it hardens into a place on a map that was never really there.

The Big Bang.base:
[[The Ninth]] Eight deep-sky bodies fill this set — a galaxy, a nebula, a comet, a pair of binary stars among them — each one a shape the universe has already finished making. The Big Bang is the ninth, and it is the one moment before any of them existed: the origin itself, not one more object beside the others. It is also, honestly, among the best-evidenced ideas in this whole encyclopedia — read off the redshift of every distant galaxy receding from every other, the leftover glow of the cosmic microwave background, and the exact ratios of hydrogen and helium the infant universe cooked in its first minutes. What the model cannot do is describe the instant itself: "singularity" marks where the equations stop giving answers, not a place anyone has observed, and what — if anything — came "before" sits past what any measurement can reach.

[[The Lesson]] The set's own vocabulary already carries a version of this dial's Lucifer-Judas axis at one remove: the outward-blazing supernova and the inward-collapsing black hole are its two readings of pride and self-erasure. The Big Bang stands beside neither pole — it is the flash before either pole existed, the single origin the explosion and the collapse both still carry an echo of.

The eight bodies here will each end differently, some quietly, some violently, some not for trillions of years yet. The ninth is there so the other eight remember that however differently they finish, every one of them started in the same single point of light.

Hades.base:
[[The Ninth]] Seven Olympians hold the week, one god to a day, and Sunday alone carries two faces — Helios in full mastery of the chariot, Phaethon in the same chariot's wreck. Hades is the ninth, and his exclusion is the whole point of him: he is the brother with no day and no light anywhere on this dial. Zeus rules the bright sky above; their third brother, Poseidon, holds the sea between; Hades keeps the one realm none of the other eight days ever touches — ruled from a throne no sun reaches. His helm, forged by the Cyclopes, does not arm him for a fight so much as let him vanish outright: a god whose defining power is choosing not to be seen.

[[The Lesson]] Where the reading lands naturally, Hades and Zeus sit at the two ends of this dial's Lucifer-Judas axis — below and above, the underworld and the bright sky — with Poseidon's sea as the unclaimed middle between them. Where the triad feels forced, he stands more simply as the unseen ninth, ruler of the one realm the other eight never visit either way.

The other eight gods each hold their hour in the light — a chariot, a forge, a garden, a throne under open sky. Hades holds none of it, and that is exactly his use: every lit hour on this dial rests over a floor no lamp reaches, and the eight are allowed to forget that only because the ninth remembers it for them.

Baldur.base:
[[The Ninth]] Seven Aesir and Sunday's own two-wolf duality — Sol driving the sun, Skoll forever a jump behind Sol — fill the Aesir set's eight regular seats. Baldur is the ninth, and unlike everything else on this ladder, he is the one Aesir the dial cannot show doing anything at all — only lying still. He is the shining, best-loved of the gods, and it is his death, not any act of his, that sets Ragnarok in motion: struck down by the one thing in all the world that had never sworn not to harm him, a dart of mistletoe, thrown by his own blind brother at Loki's guiding hand.

[[The Lesson]] No Lucifer-Judas reading is asked of Baldur, and honestly so: his story is grief and absence, not either extreme of self-regard, and forcing a pole onto a god who never acted at all would misname what actually happened to him.

The eight Aesir each act — hammer, spear, wisdom, mischief. Baldur is what they lose, and the ninth seat stays empty of any rank to remember that a world can be shaped as much by the god who stops doing anything as by all seven who keep going.

Set.base:
[[The Ninth]] Seven Theban gods hold the week, and Sunday's two faces — Ra in the day barque, Afu-Ra dimmed in the night one — complete the eight. Set is the ninth, the excluded brother, and his crime is the reason he sits outside the regular eight rather than among them: he murdered Osiris, the brother who already rules Saturday's throne in mummified peace, out of envy for that same throne. He is this pantheon's own Cain — envy turned all the way to violence rather than the slower burn the biblical story takes.

[[The Lesson]] Read as a triad rather than a single pole, Set's violent self-assertion and Osiris's total passivity in death echo this dial's Lucifer-Judas axis from opposite Egyptian ends — one brother seizing everything, the other giving everything up. Horus, the avenging son who never gets a seat on this dial either, stands as their unshown Union: the one who could have answered both extremes and appears here only as an absence twice over.

Osiris keeps Saturday's throne in peace only because someone else is willing to be the violence that peace was won against. The eight gods rule their days without a fight in sight; the ninth carries the fight so none of the other eight has to.

Crnobog.base:
[[The Ninth]] Seven Rodnovery gods and Sunday's aging Dazhbog-and-Dazhbog duality — the sun-god in his strength, the same sun-god worn down by winter — fill the set's eight regular seats. Crnobog is the ninth, the black god standing opposite every bright one on the dial, and honesty requires a caveat here the other Slavic figures don't need: Crnobog is attested mostly by one twelfth-century source, the priest Helmold writing about the Baltic Slavs of Rügen, and the tidy "black god / white god Belobog" pairing modern readers know is largely a later reconstruction, popularized well after any living Slavic paganism, rather than a documented pre-Christian doctrine.

[[The Lesson]] Where the pairing is granted, dark against bright reads as this pantheon's own version of the dial's Lucifer-Judas axis — Crnobog carrying the whole set's shadow so that none of the other seven gods has to hold any of it themselves.

The seven gods keep their sun, their thunder, their harvest lit and warm. Crnobog holds none of it, on purpose, so that what little the record actually says about him stays the coldest seat on the whole dial — and the other seven keep their fire exactly because one god was left to keep none.

The Philosopher's Stone.base:
[[The Ninth]] Seven metals — lead's dull plumb bob to gold's crucible-poured disc — fill this set's regular seats, each one a real substance real smiths and real alchemists actually worked. The Philosopher's Stone is the ninth, and unlike the seven, it never once existed: it is the imagined goal the whole historical practice of alchemy spent centuries chasing, a substance that would finish any metal's transmutation into gold and grant the Work's other promised prize, incorruptible life. Real chemistry did come out of the pursuit — acids, alloys, distillation, the vocabulary of the modern laboratory — but the Stone itself, the thing the Work was actually for, was never once produced, by anyone, in any century.

[[The Lesson]] No Lucifer-Judas reading is asked here, and rightly: this set argues transformation aimed at a single goal, not a scale stretched between two poles, and the Stone was never claimed by either end of that axis.

The seven metals are each worked toward the same one end across their own age of fire and hammer. The ninth is the end itself, never held by any of them — the mark that gave the whole Work its reason to keep going, precisely because no one ever reached it.

The Jester.base:
[[The Ninth]] The Ruler's Sunday throne and the Servant beside it anchor six working callings — Physician, Soldier, Merchant, Priest, Artist, Farmer — each with its own guild and its own canonical emblem. The Jester is the ninth, and he belongs to none of those guilds: he is the one figure at court licensed to tell the Ruler a truth no serpent-and-laurel physician, no oak-leafed soldier, no coin-counting merchant would ever risk saying aloud. The role is real history, not invention — courts across many cultures, from ancient Egypt to Tudor England, kept a fool whose motley bought him a freedom no titled courtier had.

[[The Lesson]] He reads naturally as a trinity with the Sunday pair rather than a duality: Ruler for authority, Servant for humility, and the Jester as the mirror that mocks both at once — he belongs to none of the six callings' guilds and answers to none of their masters.

The six callings each master one craft and are known by it. The Jester masters none, and that is exactly why he is the one allowed to say the true thing about all of them at once.

The Unknown God.base:
[[The Ninth]] Seven living faiths — from Freemasonry's working tools to Judaism's own unlettered star — fill this set's regular seats around the Rough Ashlar of Sunday. The Unknown God is the ninth, and he is not invented: Athens genuinely kept an altar inscribed "to an unknown god," a real precaution ancient writers besides Paul also recorded — the city hedging against having overlooked some power in its worship by leaving one altar deliberately unnamed. Paul found it standing and used it as his opening line at the Areopagus (Acts 17): the seat every creed quietly keeps open for what it does not yet know how to name.

[[The Lesson]] No duality or trinity from this dial's Lucifer-Judas scale has a natural claim on the Unknown God, and that is honestly left alone rather than forced: an altar built for what a city admits it does not know has no second pole to be read against.

The seven faiths each name what they hold sacred, in their own tongue, on their own altar. The ninth is the seat every one of them quietly leaves open — proof that even a creed confident enough to build a temple can still admit there is something past the edge of what it has named.

The Lost Mystery.base:
[[The Ninth]] Seven traditions — Mithraism's bull, Zoroastrianism's flame, Shamanism's fire, and four more — fill this set's regular seats around Corax, the raven grade that opens Sunday. The Lost Mystery is the ninth, and it names something that actually happened rather than a myth: the Eleusinian Mysteries, the rites held near Athens for roughly two thousand years, whose central revelation — whatever was actually shown to initiates inside the telesterion hall — was never written down. Thousands of people were initiated across those centuries, under a death penalty for speaking of what they saw, and by any ordinary rule of history a secret kept that long by that many people should have leaked. This one, alone among the ancient world's mystery cults, genuinely did not, and it went silent for good when Theodosius I suppressed the rites around 392 CE.

[[The Lesson]] No duality or trinity from the Lucifer-Judas scale has a natural claim here either, and for the same honest reason as Melchizedek's case elsewhere in this set: a secret that by definition left no trace behind it also left no second pole for anything to be measured against.

The seven other mysteries can each be described because someone, eventually, described them. The ninth is the one mystery that kept its actual promise — proof that this world really can hold a secret all the way to the end, and never once give it up.

Melchizedek.base:
[[The Ninth]] Joseph, Abraham and six more figures fill this set's regular seats around the Ancient of Days and the Son who serves beside him on Sunday, each one carrying a lineage the story is careful to trace — a father, a tribe, a kingdom. Melchizedek is the ninth, and Scripture goes out of its way to give him none of that: he appears in Genesis 14 as king of Salem and priest of God Most High, bringing out bread and wine to bless Abraham after battle, and Hebrews 7 later reads his sudden appearance and disappearance from the record as proof itself — "without father, without mother, without genealogy" — a priesthood older than any bloodline the other eight figures belong to.

[[The Lesson]] No duality or trinity from the Lucifer-Judas scale is asked of Melchizedek, and honestly so: his defining trait, the very thing Hebrews names him for, is having no second pole at all to be read against — not the middle of an axis, but a figure entirely outside where axes reach.

The eight other figures each carry the weight of where they came from. Melchizedek carries none of it, and blesses the man who would father all of their lines anyway — proof, in this set's own quiet way, that a blessing was never the bloodline's to withhold.

Legion.base:
[[The Ninth]] Herod's fear, Lilith's second moon, and Lucifer's and Judas's own two triangles fill this set's regular seats, each one scripture's own shadow cast by a figure already standing in the Bible theme's light. Legion is the ninth, and where that base theme's Sunday plate reads one seat wearing two balanced faces — Ancient of Days and Son, Ruler and Servant, sharing one throne without either overwhelming the other — Legion is that same arrangement failing: "my name is Legion, for we are many" (Mark 5:9), one body claimed by countless voices, held in balance by none of them.

[[The Lesson]] This is the one figure in the whole encyclopedia that reaches directly for the Union itself rather than for either triangle alone: the base Sunday seat proves two voices CAN share one throne in balance, Ancient of Days and Son, Ruler and Servant, neither drowning the other. Legion is what happens when that same seat holds not two voices in balance but every voice at once, and none of them is the one true master — the Union's own possibility, failing rather than holding.

Every other day on this dial answers to one ruler at a time, even the days built on two balanced faces. Legion is there so the rest remember that balance between two is a discipline that has to be kept — and what it looks like, lost completely, is not silence but every voice shouting from the same single throat.

The Cat.base:
[[The Ninth]] Twelve animals run the Chinese zodiac's real cycle — Rat first across the river to Pig last through the gate — each one a year, a personality, a fixed place in an order that actually governs a sixth of the world's calendars. The Cat is not one of them, and the story every version of the legend agrees on is that it should have been: in the Great Race that decided the order, the Rat tricked the Cat — waking it late, or pushing it off the Ox's broad back mid-crossing, depending on which telling you're told — so that the Cat reached the far bank too late to win a year at all. It is a folk legend explaining a real absence, not a historical account, and the details shift by region and teller; what stays constant is that cats and rats have never since been friends in the story.

[[The Lesson]] No Lucifer-Judas duality applies here, and it should not: the twelve-branch cycle this set draws from was never built on a self-love-versus-self-hate axis to begin with, so no reading from that scale has anything honest to measure against a missed boat.

The twelve animals that made the crossing each got a year with their name on it, repeating every twelve turns for as long as the calendar runs. The Cat is the one the cycle still remembers losing — proof that what a legend keeps is not only who won, but exactly who was left standing on the wrong bank.

Ophiuchus.base:
[[The Ninth]] Twelve signs divide the ecliptic into twelve equal thirty-degree arcs, from Aries to Pisces, each one carrying a classical ruling planet and a season of the year. Ophiuchus is the ninth here, and its exclusion is real astronomy rather than any moral judgment: the Sun's actual path does pass through the constellation the Serpent-Bearer traces, between Scorpius and Sagittarius, for roughly three weeks every December — a plain, well-known fact of the sky. What excludes it is calendar, not conspiracy: Western tropical astrology fixed its twelve equal arcs to the seasons around two thousand years ago and was never built to track the constellations' actual, uneven boundaries in the first place, so Ophiuchus was never "removed" so much as it was simply outside a system that was never drawing constellation lines to begin with. Occasional "thirteenth sign" headlines dramatize a detail astronomers have always known.

[[The Lesson]] Ophiuchus belongs to neither the fire triad nor the water triad the other twelve signs divide into — it straddles both, the one sign the classical four-element grouping was never built to hold. No Lucifer-Judas reading applies either, and the sheet is explicit about why: this exclusion is calendrical, not a judgment on pride or self-worth, and forcing a moral axis onto a scheduling detail would misname what actually happened here.

The twelve signs divide the year evenly and share it out, thirty degrees each, without argument. Ophiuchus is the sign-sized piece of sky the Sun genuinely crosses that the calendar simply chose not to count — proof that the wheel the other twelve ride was drawn by a ruler laid over the sky, not by the sky itself.

Gaia.base:
[[The Ninth]] Seven Olympians fill the Greek Pantheon's regular seats — Zeus at the Sunday center with his brother Hades for a shadow face, Poseidon, Artemis, Athena, Apollo, Hera and Demeter around the wheel — each seated by rank and role, and all of them younger than this ninth. Gaia is the earth itself, the first thing in Hesiod's Theogony to take shape out of Chaos, older than the sky she herself bore and any god on this dial. She mothered both lines of the week's story, the Titans the Olympians overthrew and the Olympians who overthrew them; the throne above was won on her counsel — she hid the infant Zeus and told him which prisoners to free — and the throne below is carved into her body, for every road to the underworld runs through the ground. She stands outside the week's circle because she carries both its poles at once — no seat can hold what every seat rests on.

[[The Lesson]] This Sunday already carries the dial's whole duality in one bloodline — Zeus the bright face, Hades the shadow. Gaia stands at neither pole, and the Lucifer-Judas scale has no pan for her: not a weight but the floor the balance stands on — mother of the king above, ground of the king below, the union of the week's poles rather than a third contender between them.

The eight seated figures rule what she bore. Uranus fell, Cronus fell, and Zeus's own myths keep a nervous ear out for a son repeating the pattern — the sky's dynasty changes hands in every generation. The ninth is there so the other eight remember that thrones are carved, and carving needs stone: whoever holds the sky and whoever holds the dark below stand on the same mother, and she outlasts every hand that held either.

The Pharaoh.base:
[[The Ninth]] Seven Theban gods hold the week, and Sunday's two faces — Ra in the day barque, Afu-Ra dimmed in the night one — complete the eight. The Pharaoh is the ninth, the only figure here who was neither quite a god nor merely a man: the living king, every king Egypt crowned for three thousand years, and his claim runs through two of this dial's seats at once. Crowned, he WAS Horus — the Horus name is the king's first and oldest title, older than the word "pharaoh" itself — the falcon who avenged Osiris and rules Tuesday's arm. Mummified, he became an Osiris: the funerary texts do not wish the dead king well in the afterlife, they promote him into it, addressing him by the very name of Saturday's god. Horus in life, Osiris in death — one living body wearing both faces the week keeps apart; no single day could hold him.

[[The Lesson]] The figure is imagined here as Tutankhamun — a minor king remembered mostly because his tomb alone survived intact, yet that accident of survival taught the word "pharaoh" to more of the world than every pyramid combined. This dial's Lucifer-Judas axis asks each theme for a bright face and its shadow, and Egypt answers on Sunday with one god in two boats — Ra blazing above, Afu-Ra towed through the Duat below. The Pharaoh is not asked to stand at either pole: his whole office is that axis resolved, the throne above and the throne below held in one grip — not a bright face and its shadow taking turns, but both worn at once, reign-long, by a body still breathing.

The eight gods hold their days by each being one thing completely — healer, avenger, scribe, judge. The ninth is there so the other eight remember that Egypt never asked its king to choose among them: it crowned him as the falcon and buried him as the grain god, and meant, both times, the same man.

Yggdrasil.base:
[[The Ninth]] Seven Aesir fill the Pantheon's week, one throne per day, and Sunday alone wears two faces — the Allfather enthroned, the Wanderer at the door. Yggdrasil is the ninth, and it never competes for a ninth day, because no day is left to hold it: the week itself happens inside its branches. The world-tree carries all nine worlds on one trunk — golden Asgard at the crown, Hel's cold realm sunk into the deepest root, Midgard ringed around the waist between — so every hall the eight seated gods rule from is only one address on the same tree, and none of them was ever anywhere else.

[[The Lesson]] Where the Lucifer-Judas axis usually needs two figures to complete it, the world-tree needs only itself: Asgard's golden hall sits at the crown and Hel's cold realm sits at the deepest root, the same trunk holding the pantheon's own high seat and its most feared one without favoring either. Odin's own Sunday duality — the Allfather enthroned above, the Wanderer walking below — plays out entirely inside the tree's nine worlds, one seat at the top of a single branch, one road worn root to root beneath it. Nothing here answers to a rising or a falling triangle; the tree is simply the frame both triangles would already have to be drawn inside. (Even Baldur, no longer seated here, still hangs somewhere in those branches.)

Nothing enthroned on the dial outranks the trunk it grows from — the eight seated gods each hold one hall for one day; the tree holds every hall, on every day, and was never asked to wait its turn.

Triglav.base:
[[The Ninth]] Seven seated gods and the Sunday dual of Perun above and Veles below fill this roster's eight regular places. Triglav is the ninth — and not the excluded kind: he is the Union, three heads on one body, sky, earth and underworld ruled together rather than divided between rivals. The chroniclers who watched Bishop Otto of Bamberg's mission topple his temple at Szczecin in the twelfth century record him as the highest god of the Baltic Slavs precisely because he held all three realms at once — the very axis Perun and Veles spend the whole week fighting over, already reconciled in one crowned figure. A mountain in the Julian Alps still carries his name, the tallest peak in the range, as if the land itself had voted on which summit deserved it.

[[The Lesson]] Chroniclers describe the historical idol of Triglav veiled across all three faces — a god who could see every realm at once was judged too holy to look upon the world directly. That veiling, not a withering, marks his rank: proof he outranks the seated gods rather than falling beneath them, the way an excluded ninth's bare and stripped seat would.

Every other week on this clock resolves its Sunday duality by holding the two faces apart — the bright god wears the crown, the shadow god waits at the bottom, and the dial keeps them at arm's length all seven days. The Slavic week is the only one whose ninth simply IS that pair, healed: Perun's storm is Triglav's skyward head, Veles's waters are his bowed one, and the level head between them is the earth the two of them rain and rise on — the combat myth not won by either side but outgrown.

Every seated god here answers to one hour, one color, one virtue set against one vice. Triglav answers to none of them and all of them at once — the Union that must never rank below the seven he oversees, because he is not an eighth rival seat but the shape their whole week has been tracing, veiled, patient, and outranking the throne he was cut from.

Freemasonry.base:
[[The Ninth]] Christianity's throne and its own reworked shadow face, Satanism, open Sunday two ways at once, and five more living creeds — Islam, Buddhism, Taoism, Hinduism, Sikhism — plus Judaism fill the week's remaining six seats, each one keeping its own book, day and altar. Freemasonry is the ninth, and it is neither a creed nor a rival to any of them: a candidate swears on whatever holy book his own faith already keeps open, required only to profess belief in a Supreme Being the lodge itself never names, the Great Architect of the Universe. That deliberate neutrality has made Freemasonry as much a target as a refuge across three centuries — the Catholic Church has formally warned members away from it since Clement XII's 1738 bull In Eminenti — even as its own lodges have long seated Christians, Jews, Muslims and Hindus at one working table, bound by the same oath rather than divided by their different ones.

[[The Lesson]] Freemasonry is the one ninth built to hold both of the doctrine's forms at once rather than choosing between them: the Excluded form, because no creed on this dial claims it as its own; and the Union form, because its lodge is the one room where all seven creeds' adherents have actually sat together as brothers, oath sworn before the altar rather than any one altar sworn before the oath. No reading from this dial's Lucifer-Judas scale settles which form wins, and that refusal is the whole point — a lodge was never built to rank Pride against Humility, only to seat every different answer to that question at the same table.

The seven creeds each keep a book, a day and an altar no one else may claim on their behalf. Freemasonry keeps none of that and is welcomed by all of it anyway — proof that fellowship, unlike doctrine, never had to choose a single throne to sit at, only a common floor to stand on.

The Polymath.base:
[[The Ninth]] The Ruler's Sunday throne and six working callings — Physician, Soldier, Merchant, Priest, Artist, Farmer — fill this set's regular seats, each a guild with its own tools, emblem and centuries of practice. The Polymath is the ninth, replacing the Jester the owner retired with the same blunt verdict that named his successor — 'ne može klovn da bude najviši na piramidi,' a jester cannot be the highest on the pyramid. Unlike the Jester, he is not excluded from the six estates: he holds every one of them inside a single person at once, the Leonardo archetype named for the one historical figure who genuinely worked as painter, engineer, anatomist and architect within one lifetime, filling notebooks that mix all four disciplines on the same page.

[[The Lesson]] No single pole of this dial's Lucifer-Judas scale has an honest claim on the Polymath, and the doctrine's own law explains why: the Union must never rank below the seated figures it completes, and a figure built from the sum of all seven estates cannot be measured against any one estate's own virtue or vice without shrinking back into it. He is not proud in the Ruler's particular way, nor humble in any single Servant's, because he was never only one of them to begin with.

The six callings each master one craft and are known by it, generation after generation, guild after guild. The Polymath masters all six at once and belongs to none of their registers — and keeps one relic of the calling he replaced: a small bell, the last thread of a jester's motley, the one privilege the fool once held that he alone still keeps, permission to tell the throne a truth none of the six specialists could afford to risk telling it themselves.

The Holy Trinity.base:
[[The Ninth]] Ancient of Days and the Son who serves quietly at his side share Sunday's own two faces, and six more figures — Mary, David, Moses, Solomon, Adam and Eve, Joseph — fill the base Bible theme's remaining seats, each carrying a lineage the story traces with some care. The Holy Trinity is the ninth, and it is the owner's own worked example of the Union form, offered before any other theme had one: 'gde je otac nedeljna slika, a sin njegov dual, deveti je Sveto Trojstvo — unija samog para' — where the Father is the Sunday plate and the Son is its dual, the ninth is not a third figure beside the pair but the union of the pair itself. Father, Son and Spirit as one has been recited as doctrine since the Nicene Creed in 325, without the church ever needing to rank the three persons against one another.

[[The Lesson]] This is the one figure built to complete its own seat rather than contest it: the Ancient of Days and the Son already prove, every Sunday, that Ruler and Servant can share one throne without either overwhelming the other, and the Trinity is that same proof carried one step further — not a third vote cast to break a tie, but the same balance read, finally, as a single indivisible name. Per the doctrine's own law the Union may never rank below the figures it stands above; here it does not even need to compete with them, since it was never a separate figure to begin with.

Every other ninth in this encyclopedia stands outside its set's regular seats, excluded from all of them or completing a place none of the others could fill. The Holy Trinity is the one ninth built entirely out of a seat already on the dial — proof that the highest place a true Union can reach is not a new throne beside the old one, but the old one, at last, read whole.

The Ninth Circle.base:
[[The Ninth]] Herod's fear, Lilith's second moon, and Lucifer's and Judas's own two triangles fill this set's regular seats, each one scripture's own shadow cast by a figure the base Bible theme already keeps standing in its light. The Ninth Circle is the ninth, and it is the owner's second worked example of the Union form, this time as a place rather than a person: 'nema osobe koja je i Lucifer i Juda — ali Pakao ih drži oboje, na samom dnu, po Danteu' — no mythology offers one figure who is both Lucifer and Judas at once, but Dante's own geography never needed one. Inferno's frozen ninth circle, Cocytus, holds both together at the very bottom of Hell, Lucifer's three mouths working slowly on Judas Iscariot alongside Brutus and Cassius for eternity (Inferno XXXIV).

[[The Lesson]] The Ninth Circle is this dial's most literal reading of its own Lucifer-Judas scale, the only ninth that answers the scale directly rather than stepping outside its reach: the pit does not stand beside pride and despair the way every other seated figure does, it stands beneath both at once, holding the self-exalting fall of one and the self-erasing collapse of the other in the same three jaws together. Per the doctrine's own law the Union must never rank below the figures it completes, and nothing here even attempts the comparison — the pit does not need to outrank Lucifer and Judas, since Dante's own poem already put both of them permanently inside it.

The eight seated figures each carry one shape of scripture's own darkness — a tyrant's fear, a second moon, a triangle's pride or a triangle's despair. The Ninth Circle is the floor sitting underneath every one of them, a place Dante's own poem insists is not a metaphor but an actual location on the map of the afterlife — proof that even a scale built with two clear, opposite poles eventually needs one seat carved deep enough to hold both ends down together, at once.

Zealandia.base:
[[The Ninth]] Zealandia is the Unfound — the eighth continent almost nobody has heard of, because 94% of it is under the sea. It is real continental crust, a drowned landmass roughly half the size of Australia with New Zealand and New Caledonia as its few peaks that break the surface; the rest is a sunken country a kilometer down. Geologists argued over it for decades and only in 2017 agreed, formally, that it is a continent — a whole eighth land recognized within living memory, hidden in plain sight the entire time.

[[The Continent That Was Not Found]] That is why it holds the Ninth seat, the theme's own version of the Canon's Unfound: a true continent that was there all along, never found by the eight, waiting under the water. It was once above the waves; it has been unfound for ages; and the slow arithmetic of the plates may lift it again.

Pangea.base:
[[The Deep-Time Ninth]] Pangea is the deep-time face of the Ninth, and it shows in Zealandia's place only when the sky is doing something — an eclipse, a solstice or equinox, a full or new moon, the days the dial itself marks as turning points. It is the supercontinent that was once all: three hundred million years ago every land on this theme's wheel was fused into one, the six weekday continents a single body before the plates tore them apart and set them drifting to their separate weekdays.

[[Was One, Is Many, Will Be One]] The story is Zealandia's, told at the scale of the whole planet: it was once everything; it split and was scattered; and by the supercontinent cycle — the slow gathering that has happened before and will happen again — the wanderers will one day reconvene into a single land. The Unfound at the scale of all things: the world was one, is many, and will be one again.

Pegasus.base:
[[The Ninth]] Eight monsters fill this set and every one of them has a seat, a vice and a day. Pegasus has none of the three, and that is the seat: he is born out of Medusa's death — the blood of the Monday arm — and belongs from that moment to neither line the week is built from. He is not a monster, having harmed no one and been hunted by nobody; he is not a god, having no cult, no domain and no day. The Excluded kind of Ninth, in the canon's own terms: a figure the story cannot do without and the circle cannot seat.

[[The Lesson]] What he does have is the one office none of the eight can hold — carriage. Bellerophon rides him against the Chimera and then tries to ride him to Olympus, and the myth is exact about the outcome: the horse arrives, the rider does not. That is the ninth's whole argument against the eight. Every seated figure on this wheel is defined by what it takes from whoever comes near it; Pegasus is defined by what he carries, and by the fact that the carrying has a limit which is not his fault.

The canon holds that the Ninth is never less important than the seated eight, and here that is the plainest case in the book: the set's most famous creature is the one with no day, because a week has six arms and a center, while the thing born out of a week's worst hour belongs to the sky between them.

Buddha.base:
[[The Ninth]] Eight figures fill this cast and every one of them holds a day, a virtue and a vice. The Buddha holds none of the three, and the reason is structural rather than modest: he is the only being in the story who can tell the true Monkey King from the false one, which means he cannot sit inside the circle whose two faces he adjudicates. The canon calls this the Excluded kind of Ninth — a figure the story cannot do without and the week cannot seat.

[[The Lesson]] The Ninth seat's own sin, in this book, is WISH: the appetite that has no object left and therefore never closes. Every seated figure here is defined by something wanted — a title, a reunion, a harvest, a meal, a verdict. The Buddha is the one being in the cast defined by having extinguished the wanting rather than by having satisfied it, which is what nirvana literally names: a blowing-out. He holds the Ninth by conquest, then, and not merely by exclusion — the seat outside the eight, held by the one who stopped needing any of them.

The same episode makes both claims at once. Heaven's instruments failed on the two monkeys because instruments compare properties, and the two had identical properties; the Buddha answered because he was not comparing. The canon holds that the Ninth is never less important than the seated eight, and this cast makes the strongest form of that argument in the book: the week's central dispute is decided from outside the week.

The Founder.base:
[[The Ninth]] Six offices hold the week and a dual holds Sunday, and every one of them exists on the organisation chart. The Founder does not. The seat is the Unfound kind of Ninth in this cast's own vocabulary: the origin the structure no longer names, present in every company that has one and listed in none. Whoever started the thing either left, was removed, sold, died, or is still there under a title that no longer describes what happened.

[[The Lesson]] The eight seated offices are all specialisations — each one a defensible answer to a question the company already knows it has. The Founder is the opposite kind of thing: the person who acted before there was any question, any function, any evidence, or anybody to allocate. That is why the seat cannot be inside the circle. A corporation is an institution for repeating what works, and its origin is by definition the one moment when nothing was yet known to work.

The canon holds that the Ninth is never less important than the seated eight, and here the claim is almost administrative: all six functions and both faces of Sunday are answers to a question somebody asked first, and the chart that lists them has no column for the asking.

Turalyon.base:
[[The Ninth]] Eight seats hold this cast and every one of them is a name the Alliance says out loud. Turalyon is the ninth because for a thousand years he was a name it had stopped saying. Lothar's lieutenant, who took command of the army the hour Lothar fell at Blackrock Spire and finished the war with it, he then followed the Sons of Lothar through the Dark Portal and did not return in any lifetime that remembered him. The Excluded kind of Ninth, in the canon's own terms: a figure the story cannot do without and the circle cannot seat.

[[The Lesson]] What he holds that none of the eight can is continuity without a witness. Every seated figure here is defined by an act somebody saw — a refusal at Stratholme, a wall at Gilneas, a city built at Theramore. Turalyon spent a thousand years keeping the same oath in a place with no Alliance in it, no relief coming, and no possibility of the account ever being settled. That is the seat's whole argument against the eight: a virtue that requires an audience is a performance, and this is the one figure whose service had none.

The canon holds that the Ninth is never less important than the seated eight, and here the claim is almost administrative: the Alliance that Varian rebuilt and Anduin inherited was still, the entire time, being defended somewhere off the map by a man neither of them had met.

Rexxar.base:
[[The Ninth]] Eight seats hold this cast and every one of them belongs to somebody's people — a clan, a tribe, a cartel, a herd. Rexxar belongs to none. Half orc and half ogre, raised by neither, he is the Horde's champion by deed and its member by no other claim, and he has spent the whole story living in open country with beasts rather than in any of the cities he has saved. The Excluded kind of Ninth, in the canon's own terms: a figure the story cannot do without and the circle cannot seat.

[[The Lesson]] What he holds that none of the eight can is loyalty with no membership underneath it. Every seated figure here is a representative: Baine speaks for the tauren, Vol'jin for the Darkspear, Gallywix for a cartel, Thrall for an idea he invented. Their virtues are all, in part, the virtues of an office. Rexxar has no office and no constituency, and he came when Thrall's new nation was surrounded and had nothing to offer him. A service that cannot be explained by belonging is the one thing the seated eight are structurally unable to demonstrate.

The canon holds that the Ninth is never less important than the seated eight, and this cast makes the point twice over: the Horde's founding myth is a coalition of peoples, and its purest act of loyalty was performed by the one man who is not a people at all.

Medivh.base:
[[The Ninth]] Eight seats hold this cast and every one of them chose what it became. Medivh is the ninth because he is the only figure here who was decided before he was born: the last Guardian of Tirisfal, carrying Sargeras's spirit from the moment of his conception because his mother had killed the titan's body and taken the wound into her own line. He opened the Dark Portal, brought the orcs to Azeroth, and was killed by his own apprentice for it. The Excluded kind of Ninth, in the canon's own terms: a figure the story cannot do without and the circle cannot seat.

[[The Lesson]] What the ninth seat holds here is the question the other eight are constructed to avoid. Every seated figure is argued from a decision — a drink accepted, a blade taken up, a council founded, a whisper obeyed — and the whole moral architecture of this cast depends on those decisions being real. Medivh's were not, and he is nevertheless responsible for more of the setting's ruin than any of them. Then, freed by his own death, he came back as an unrecognised prophet and assembled the alliance that beat the thing he had let in.

The canon holds that the Ninth is never less important than the seated eight, and here it is the plainest case in the book: the cast's greatest catastrophe and its most improbable rescue were performed by the same man, and neither one is cleanly his.

NetWatch.base:
[[The Ninth]] Eight seats hold this cast and every one of them is a name written on a wall somewhere in Night City. NetWatch is the ninth because it is a power with no ground at all. It is the transnational agency that polices the Net and maintains the Blackwall, the barrier standing between human networks and what the DataKrash left on the other side, and its jurisdiction is the one thing in this setting that is genuinely everywhere and locatable nowhere. The Excluded kind of Ninth, in the canon's own terms: a body the story cannot do without and the circle cannot seat.

[[The Lesson]] What it holds that none of the eight can is authority without territory. Every seated faction here is defined by an address — a district, a strip, a plant, a tower — and the whole argument of a gang is that it will still be at that address tomorrow. NetWatch has no address, takes no ground, and is nevertheless the only party in the cast whose failure would end the setting rather than rearrange it. That is the seat's argument against the eight: they are fighting over the surface of a city standing on a wall none of them maintains.

The canon holds that the Ninth is never less important than the seated eight, and here the claim is almost administrative. Wednesday's netrunners are famous for exactly one thing — going to the wall and coming back — and the wall they go to is somebody else's work.

V.base:
[[The Ninth]] Eight seats hold this cast and every one of them is a person the city can name. V is the ninth because V is the one the city cannot — a mercenary who arrives with no standing, acquires all of it in a matter of weeks, and spends the whole of that time being overwritten by somebody else's personality construct. The canon keeps two kinds of Ninth, the Excluded and the Union, and this seat is unusual in being both at once: excluded because the circle has no chair for the person it is all happening to, and a union because two people are demonstrably occupying one skull.

[[The Lesson]] What V holds that none of the eight can is the unfinished state. Every seated figure here is defined by something already done — a clinic built, a job taken, a band outlived, a tower entered — and can therefore be argued about. V is defined by a deadline. The seat's whole claim against the eight is that identity is the one possession in this setting that can be taken by a piece of hardware, and that everybody else's biography is being read by somebody who may not have one by the end of the month.

The canon holds that the Ninth is never less important than the seated eight, and here it is barely a claim at all: every relationship in this cast runs through the figure that has no seat, and the reason the identity is kept deliberately unresolved is that the seat is about the condition rather than the person.

Alt Cunningham.base:
[[The Ninth]] Eight seats hold this cast and every one of them is occupied by somebody with a body. Alt Cunningham is the ninth because she has not had one since 2013. A netrunner who co-authored the program that copies a mind out of a person, she was killed by the corporation that wanted it and went into the Net as the thing her own work made possible; what exists now is beyond the Blackwall and is not, by its own account, her. The Excluded kind of Ninth, in the canon's own terms: a figure the story cannot do without and the circle cannot seat.

[[The Lesson]] What she holds that none of the eight can is the demonstration. Every seated figure in this cast is arguing about power over other people; she is the proof of what the power in question actually is, because the program that took her is the same one the Sunday throne used to arrange its own survival. The seat's whole claim against the eight is that they are all negotiating inside a technology one of them invented and none of them controls.

[[The Second Ninth]] The seat rotates in lockstep with the Throne and the Mirror. On the alternate turn it is held by Rache Bartmoss, the netrunner who set off the DataKrash and destroyed the old Net, and whose body is kept frozen while whatever is left of him sprawls through the wreckage he made. The pairing is exact: she was taken by the wall and he is why there had to be one.

The canon holds that the Ninth is never less important than the seated eight, and here it is not a claim but a chronology — everything this cast fights over runs on infrastructure these two built and then fell into.

Yoda.base:
[[The Ninth]] Eight seats hold this cast and Yoda occupies none of them, because for the entire span the dial reads he is not in the story the galaxy can see. Nine hundred years old, the order's own senior master, he is believed dead by every party in the conflict and lives on a planet no chart marks. That is the Excluded kind of Ninth in the canon's exact sense: a figure the story cannot do without and the circle has no chair for.

[[The Lesson]] What he holds that none of the eight can is the verdict. He presided over the institution that failed to see what in front of it for a decade, and his exile is not primarily a hiding place — it is a sentence he passed on himself and then served. The seat's claim against the eight is that the catastrophe was not an ambush but an oversight, and the only member of the cast senior enough to be responsible for it is the one who removed himself from the board.

[[Outside the Circle]] The canon holds that the Ninth is never less important than the seated eight, and here the arithmetic is explicit: the two figures who finish the story are both trained by him, one publicly and one in a swamp, and neither training happens on any of the eight arms.

*"For in much wisdom is much grief: and he that increaseth knowledge increaseth sorrow"* (Ecclesiastes 1:18).

Darth Plagueis.base:
[[The Ninth]] Eight seats hold this cast and every one of them is occupied by somebody the story shows. Darth Plagueis is the ninth because he exists in it only as a story being told — described once, in a single conversation, by the man who murdered him, to the man being recruited. The Excluded kind of Ninth in the canon's exact sense: a figure the whole cast descends from and the circle cannot seat, because nothing he did happens on screen.

[[The Lesson]] What he holds that none of the eight can is the premise. The entire Sunday recruitment turns on one claim about him — that he had learned to prevent a death — and the claim is made by the only witness, who is also the beneficiary, to a listener who cannot check it. Whether it is true is never established, and the seat's argument is that it did not need to be: a story about a dead master, told at the right moment, bought this cast its Servant.

[[The Rule Turned On Its Author]] He is also the doctrine's own receipt. The Rule of Two requires the apprentice to replace the master, and the master who taught it best was killed in his sleep by the student he taught it to — which is the one event in this cast that nobody arranged, because the arrangement had been made generations earlier and simply matured.

*"Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein"* (Proverbs 26:27).

The Ghosts.base:
[[The Ninth]] Eight seats hold this cast and every one of them is held by a living person. The Ghosts are the ninth because they are the accumulated dead of the entire story, still acting in it — the voices that reach the Sunday throne at the moment it has nothing left, and the reason it stands up. The canon is explicit that a Ninth need not be a person: a place, an event or a concept qualifies, and this seat is a chorus.

[[The Lesson]] What they hold that none of the eight can is the continuity. Every seated figure in this cast is arguing about inheritance — who is owed one, who refuses one, who destroys one — and this seat is the answer the argument keeps circling: what is actually inherited is not a name or a bloodline but a body of deeds that other people did first. The Excluded kind of Ninth in the canon's terms, excluded by the plainest possible criterion, and nevertheless decisive.

[[The Second Face]] The seat turns, and its other face is Exegol — a world no chart admits exists, holding a fleet and a lineage that everybody believed finished. The pairing is the seat's whole argument stated twice: the dead do not stop acting, and that is true of both sides. One face is what the story inherited from the people who were right; the other is what it inherited from the people who were not. This is the same shape the instrument already uses for the Continents' own Ninth, where a hidden true thing gives way to a rarer, older one — a light and a dark reading of the identical seat.

*"Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses"* (Hebrews 12:1).

Exegol.base:
[[The Ninth's Other Face]] The seat that reads The Ghosts by day reads Exegol by night — the instrument's own daylight/night law reaching the Ninth itself, not just the Throne. No chart admits Exegol exists: it is a world erased from every record the Republic and the Empire it curdled into ever kept, found only by following a legend nobody in power believed. It is the Excluded kind of Ninth twice over — excluded from the map, and excluded from the count of eight the same way the Ghosts are, because a world is not a person either.

[[What It Holds]] Where the Ghosts are continuity — the dead who keep acting because their deeds outlive them — Exegol is the opposite inheritance: a lineage the story had already declared finished, kept alive in secret past every ending it was given, surfacing at the exact moment the eight seated figures believe the account is closed. A fleet built in the dark answers a fleet the light side never saw coming.

[[Day and Night, Not Good and Evil]] The seat does not turn on virtue — the canon's Excluded Ninths rarely do. It turns on WHEN. The Ghosts answer at the seat's own noon, the hour the Sunday throne has nothing left and needs its dead; Exegol answers at midnight, the hour the story's oldest enemy chooses to prove it was never dead at all. Same seat, same argument about what outlives the living, read once by daylight and once by dark.

*"For there is nothing hid, which shall not be manifested; neither was any thing kept secret, but that it should come abroad"* (Mark 4:22).

Dionysus.base:
[[The Figure]] Wine, theatre, ecstasy and the crowd that loses itself in them — Dionysus is the Olympian who arrives from outside the city and takes it apart to remake it. He is the twice-born god: torn from his dying mortal mother Semele and carried to term in Zeus's own thigh, killed and returned, god by his father and mortal by his mother, holding both natures in one body — the very thing Euripides' Bacchae calls the gentlest and most terrible of gods.

[[The Story]] On this dial he was argued for the ninth seat itself — the twice-born as the Greek Union figure, both natures at once — and he lost it honestly to Gaia, the earth that mothers gods and Titans alike. He has a claim on Thursday too: the yellow seat's overflow, Excess, is his by nature and Joy his weather. But a seat is measured by a figure's rank, not by the vice it fits, and Apollo — Delphi, prophecy, music given freely — outranks him on fame and breadth. Twice considered, twice passed over: exactly the shape of a figure too large for the encyclopedia to lose and too particular for any single day to hold.

[[The Lesson]] Every other Olympian keeps one hour and one temper. Dionysus is the one who dissolves the boundary — between god and man, between the reveller and the reveller beside him, between grief and joy at the same festival. The dial seats the gods who keep their station; it remembers Dionysus as the force that visits to unseat them, and is the truer for admitting it could never sit him down.

Hephaestus.base:
[[The Figure]] The smith of the gods, the one Olympian who works — lame in both feet, cast out of heaven by his own mother Hera for the flaw of his birth, and greater at the forge than any whole-limbed god above him. His hands made the armour of Achilles, the necklace of Harmonia, and the very thrones the others sit on.

[[The Story]] The craft seat on this dial is Wednesday — the making mind, Mercury's purple — and it went to Athena, wisdom itself, with Hermes keeping the Planetary chair; the forge lost to the workshop of the intellect. So the god who literally built Olympus keeps no day on the dial Olympus decorates. Homer gives him the Iliad's most famous set-piece, the Shield of Achilles hammered with the whole world — the earth, the sky, two cities, a wedding and a war — the maker rendering everything he is never invited to rule.

[[The Lesson]] The lesson is the oldest one about makers: the work outlasts and outshines the standing of the one who made it. Seven gods hold their hours in the light; the eighth forged the frame those hours hang in, and the dial keeps him here to remember that the instrument is always more famous than its smith.

Hestia.base:
[[The Figure]] The eldest of the Olympians and the stillest — goddess of the hearth, the fire at the centre of every house and every city, and the one great Greek deity with almost no myths, because she never leaves home to make them. First-born of Cronus and swallowed first, last brought back up, she is the beginning and the end of her own generation.

[[The Story]] Hers is the seat given away on purpose. When the tally of the great gods filled and Dionysus needed a place at the table of the twelve, it is Hestia — in the tellings that count her among them — who yields her throne and steps back to tend the fire, keeping the peace of the house rather than her rank in it. On a dial built entirely of seats, she is the goddess who chose the centre over a chair, and so she belongs to no arm and to all of them at once: the Hearth the Trinity's own family reading places at the middle, the fire that warms where the Eye watches.

[[The Lesson]] The eight seats compete for their hours; Hestia keeps the flame they all come home to. The dial cannot seat her because a hearth is not a station — it is the still point the stations turn around, and the surest sign of her presence on the instrument is that its centre is never empty.

Set.base:
[[The Figure]] The red god of the desert, the storm and disorder — Set is Egypt's necessary violence, the brother who murdered Osiris out of envy for the throne that already rules Saturday in mummified peace. He is this pantheon's own Cain: envy carried all the way to the killing, rather than the slower burn the Bible's story takes.

[[The Story]] For a while he held the ninth seat as the excluded brother, and the doctrine moved him aside: the ninth is now the Pharaoh — Horus in life and Osiris in death, the throne above and below in one living body — and Set retires here, to the wider circle, his murder-story surviving intact inside the Osiris and Horus articles regardless. Read across the dial, he and Osiris echo its Lucifer–Judas axis from opposite Egyptian ends — one brother seizing everything, the other giving everything up — with Horus, the avenging son, as the union neither seat shows.

[[The Lesson]] Osiris keeps Saturday's throne in peace only because someone was willing to be the violence that peace was won against. Every lit hour on this dial rests over that arrangement; Set is kept in the encyclopedia so the eight seated gods are never allowed to forget who carried the fight for them — even after his own seat was taken away.

Nut.base:
[[The Figure]] The sky herself — Nut is the goddess whose star-scattered body arches over the whole world, toes at one horizon and fingertips at the other, held up off her husband Geb the earth by their father Shu the air. Mother of Osiris, Isis, Set and Nephthys: the entire drama of the Egyptian week is born from her.

[[On the Dial]] No god stands closer to what this instrument actually draws. Each dusk Nut swallows the sun into her mouth; it travels the length of her body through the night and she gives birth to it again at dawn — the exact day-and-night arc the dial lays top to bottom, noon high in the light, midnight buried at the base. She is the movement the clock measures, which is precisely why no single hour can seat her: a figure who IS the turning cannot be pinned to one point on the turn.

[[The Lesson]] The eight seated gods each own a station along the arc. Nut is the arc.
