[[The Forces Behind]] A week held by the powers that move behind the gangs and the street alike: Songbird on Monday's Fear, Adam Smasher on Tuesday's Wrath, Dexter DeShawn on Wednesday's Greed, Solomon Reed on Thursday's Generosity, Evelyn Parker on Friday's Love, Takemura on Saturday's Patience. The seating rule is the one this whole instrument runs on — each figure is placed against the pair the seat already names, and argued from a deed rather than from a reputation. This cast is the one that most often sits on the shadow half of the bundle, which is what a power looks like from underneath.

[[Sunday's Two Faces]] Sunday is a founder and his killer: Saburo Arasaka, who built a corporation that outlives states and arranged not to accept the one limit everybody else does, against Yorinobu, who spent his life denying the house and then took the chair. Alt Cunningham is the ninth, a netrunner with no body left at all.

[[The Lockstep]] All three of this cast's central seats rotate, and they rotate together: the Throne, the Mirror and the Ninth each hold two figures, and because every one of them holds exactly two, the shared date rule lands on the same index for all three on any given day. Saburo, Yorinobu and Alt stand together; Rosalind Myers, Kurt Hansen and Rache Bartmoss stand together — one empire and its rival, argued through the same three offices.

This is one of three casts riding the same nine seats. Gangs holds them with the factions that own the ground and Street with the people; the seats do not move, only who is sitting in them.

sw_jedi.title: Star Wars Jedi
sw_jedi.base:
[[The Council of Lights]] A week held by the side that loses for most of the story and is right for all of it: Obi-Wan Kenobi on Monday's Fear, Leia Organa on Tuesday's Wrath, Han Solo on Wednesday's Greed, Qui-Gon Jinn on Thursday's Excess, Padmé Amidala on Friday's Jealousy, Chewbacca on Saturday's Envy. The seating rule is the one this whole instrument runs on — each figure is placed against the pair the seat already names, and argued from a deed rather than from a reputation. This cast is the one that most often sits on the bright half of the bundle, and the interest is in what it costs each of them to stay there.

[[Sunday's Two Faces]] Sunday is a father and the son who refused to kill him: Luke Skywalker, who throws the weapon away at the moment the victory is available, against Vader, who spent twenty years carrying out another man's decisions and reversed it once. Yoda is the ninth, nine hundred years old and believed dead by everyone.

[[The Repeats Are Deliberate]] Two figures of this cast sit again in the Dyad cast, thirty years older and on different arms — the instrument's rule is that three sets on one seat are three different people, and an age of a person is one of them. Leia at nineteen is argued from an interrogation; Leia at fifty-odd is argued from what she hands over. Neither article restates the other.

This is one of three casts riding the same nine seats. The Sith cast holds them with the men who won, and the Dyad with the generation that inherited the result; the seats do not move, only who is sitting in them.

sw_sith.title: Star Wars Sith
sw_sith.base:
[[The Rule of Two]] A week held by the side that wins: Tarkin on Monday's Fear, General Grievous on Tuesday's Wrath, Jabba the Hutt on Wednesday's Greed, Count Dooku on Thursday's Excess, Maul on Friday's Jealousy, Boba Fett on Saturday's Envy. The seating rule is the one this whole instrument runs on — each figure is placed against the pair the seat already names, and argued from a deed rather than from a reputation. This cast sits on the shadow half of every bundle, which is what makes it the most useful of the three: a vice is easier to define when somebody is administering it deliberately.

[[Sunday's Two Faces]] Sunday is a master and his apprentice: Palpatine, who was voted into every office he ever held and used each one to dismantle the body that granted it, against Anakin Skywalker, recruited at nine and prepared for over a decade. Darth Plagueis is the ninth, a figure the story describes exactly once, in a conversation, and never shows.

[[The Doctrine]] The lineage this cast is named for holds that there are always exactly two — a master and an apprentice, and the apprentice replaces the master by killing him. Three of the nine seats here are occupied by men who did precisely that, in sequence, and the Sunday dual is one link of the chain caught mid-transfer.

This is one of three casts riding the same nine seats. The Jedi cast holds them with the side that loses and is right, and the Dyad with the generation that inherits the result; the seats do not move, only who is sitting in them.

sw_dyad.title: Star Wars Dyad
sw_dyad.base:
[[The Dyad]] The only mixed cast of the three: light and dark held together, because the seat that decides it is itself dual. Rose Tico on Monday's Fear, Finn and Phasma on Tuesday's Wrath, Maz Kanata and DJ on Wednesday's Greed, Leia on Thursday's Excess, Han on Friday's Jealousy, General Hux on Saturday's Envy. The seating rule is the one this whole instrument runs on — each figure is placed against the pair the seat already names, and argued from a deed rather than from a reputation.

[[Sunday's Two Faces]] Sunday is the bond the films name outright: Rey, a scavenger with no inheritance who takes a name rather than finding one, against Kylo Ren, an heir with every inheritance who destroys each of them and serves somebody at every point. The Ghosts are the ninth — the accumulated dead of the whole story, still acting — and the seat turns to Exegol, a world no chart admits, when the rotation reaches it.

[[Three Seats That Turn]] Tuesday, Wednesday and the Ninth each hold more than one occupant, and the dial shows one of them at a time. The label names every member and the article argues all of them, so whichever occupant the dial reaches on a given day, the text has already made its case for that one. Two of the three are pairs of people; the third is a pair of places, which the canon permits — a Ninth need not be a person at all.

[[The Repeats Are Deliberate]] Leia and Han sit again in the Jedi cast, thirty years younger and on different arms. The instrument's rule is that three sets on one seat are three different people, and an age of a person is one of them: the younger articles argue an interrogation and a smuggler's return, and these argue what a parent hands over.

planets.title: The Week's Duality
planets.base: [[Sun and Shadow]] Every themed week folds its seventh day in two: a bright Ruler face and a Servant/shadow face sharing the same seat. On the neutral Planets roster this is the Sun itself and the Eclipsed Sun — the ordinary disc, then the same disc with the Moon drawn dark across it, the one day a year the ruler visibly yields.

planet_signs.title: The Week's Duality
planet_signs.base: [[Sun and Shadow]] The SAME duality as the Planets topic, read in glyphs instead of photographs — the sun sign beside its own eclipsed mark, the one moment a year the ruling glyph visibly dims.

greek.title: The Week's Duality
greek.base: [[Helios and Phaethon]] Every theme folds Sunday into two faces sharing one throne. Helios is the Ruler who has driven the sun's chariot since before memory, its reins second nature; Phaethon is his own son, given the reins for one day and unable to hold them, scorching a black streak across the sky before he falls. Mastery and its nearest, most human failure, on the same seat.

norse.title: The Week's Duality
norse.base: [[Sól and Sköll]] Sunday's two faces are a race, not a throne room: Sól drives the sun-wagon across the sky one length ahead of Sköll, the wolf born to chase and, at Ragnarök, finally catch her. The Ruler here is defined entirely by the Servant hunting her — the whole Norse sky runs on that unfinished chase.

egypt.title: The Week's Duality
egypt.base: [[Ra and Afu-Ra]] Sunday folds into the sun god's own two half-days: Ra crossing the visible sky by light, then Afu-Ra — the ram-headed night form of the SAME god — rowing his barque through the Duat's twelve dark hours, fighting Apep the chaos-serpent every single night so dawn can return him whole. Not two persons — one god's day and night faces.

slavic.title: The Week's Duality
slavic.base: [[Young and Old Dažbog]] Sunday's two faces are one god's own year: the young Dažbog crowned each spring, giving sun and warmth, aging across the months into the old Dažbog winter wears down to almost nothing — then reborn at the next solstice. The Ruler IS his own Servant, on a longer clock than a day.

greek_pantheon.title: The Week's Duality
greek_pantheon.base: [[Zeus and Hades]] The Pantheon's Sunday splits the two brothers who drew lots for the world after the Titans fell: Zeus won the sky and the throne, Hades the dead and everything beneath the earth — not a fall, not a punishment, just the world divided between equals by chance.

norse_pantheon.title: The Week's Duality
norse_pantheon.base: [[Odin and the Wanderer]] The Pantheon's Sunday keeps ONE god in two postures: Odin enthroned in Asgard, all-seeing, and the Wanderer — the same Allfather in a grey cloak and wide hat, walking Midgard's roads incognito, testing hosts and gathering wisdom nobody on a throne could ever learn.

egypt_pantheon.title: The Week's Duality
egypt_pantheon.base: [[Ra and Afu-Ra]] The Pantheon closes on the SAME pair the Planetary run does — Egypt's sun never needed a second face invented for it: Ra by day, Afu-Ra rowing the Duat by night, one god, two crossings.

slavic_pantheon.title: The Week's Duality
slavic_pantheon.base: [[Perun and Veles]] The Pantheon's Sunday is the oldest quarrel in the Slavic sky: Perun the thunder-god above, Veles the horned god of cattle, water and the dead below — their yearly battle, Perun's lightning striking Veles back into the underworld each spring, is the myth every storm reenacts.

alchemy.title: The Week's Duality
alchemy.base: [[Gold and Raw Ore]] Sunday folds the Great Work itself in two: refined Gold, the goal every alchemist's furnace chased, beside the Raw Ore it began as — unsmelted, unworked, dug out of the same earth. The whole theme's seven metals are really one question asked seven times: what does this base matter become when it is finished?

japan.title: The Week's Duality
japan.base: [[Amaterasu and Ama-no-Iwato]] Sunday's two faces retell Japan's own founding myth: Amaterasu radiant on her throne, and the Ama-no-Iwato, the cave she once sealed herself inside after her brother's cruelty — plunging the whole world into darkness until the other gods' laughter drew her back out. The sun goddess and the one door that can hide her.

religion.title: The Week's Duality
religion.base: [[Christianity and Satanism]] Sunday folds the theme's own central argument in two: Christianity keeping the day of the Resurrection, Satanism reading every one of its symbols in reverse on the same seat. Not a second faith so much as the first faith's own mirror, defined entirely by what it inverts.

religion_alt.title: The Week's Duality
religion_alt.base: [[Mithraism and Corax]] Sunday's two faces are one cult's own ladder: Mithraism as the Sun-soldier's faith entire — Sol Invictus, the bull, the seven grades of initiation — and Corax, the Raven, the LOWEST of those seven grades, the newest initiate who has not yet climbed toward the light he serves.

profession.title: The Week's Duality
profession.base: [[Ruler and Servant]] Sunday's two faces are the theme's own thesis stated plainly: the Ruler who commands and the Servant who carries the command out, one throne built from both halves of every hierarchy the six weekday professions serve.

wolf.title: The Week's Duality
wolf.base: [[Alpha and Omega]] Sunday's two faces are the pack's own two ends: Alpha leading the hunt at the front, Omega absorbing the pack's tension at the back — the whole rank order exists to be measured between them (Sigma, the pack's Ninth, is neither end — the wolf with no pack at all).

bee.title: The Week's Duality
bee.base: [[Queen and Cleaner]] Sunday's two faces are the hive's own beginning and its newest daughter: the Queen who founded every cell in the comb, and the Cleaner tending the humblest work at that same founding cell — the hive's whole history compressed into one wall.

elephant.title: The Week's Duality
elephant.base: [[Matriarch and Memory]] Sunday's two faces are the living herd and the dead one still leading it: the Matriarch who decides where the herd walks today, and Memory — the map of every drought, predator and grave she carries from matriarchs before her. The herd's whole intelligence is what it refuses to forget.

bible.title: The Week's Duality
bible.base: [[Ancient of Days and Son]] Sunday's two faces are not opposites but the Trinity's own pair: the Ancient of Days on His eternal throne, and the Son seated at His right hand — Father and Son sharing one seat the way this whole theme's Sunday shares its throne with every OTHER theme's Ruler and Servant, argued honestly rather than forced into a mold that does not fit it.

bible2.title: The Week's Duality
bible2.base: [[Abraham and Isaac]] Sunday's two faces are father and bound son: Abraham who believed enough to raise the knife, and Isaac who was spared at the altar's edge — obedience and mercy sharing one seat, the same seat every OTHER theme's Ruler and Servant occupy, read here through its own story instead of forced into theirs.

bible_dark.title: The Week's Duality
bible_dark.base: [[Lucifer and Judas]] Sunday's two faces are the theme's own twin founding falls: Lucifer's rebellion against Heaven out of pride, Judas' betrayal of one friend out of greed — the Two Triangles' own scale (see The Human Wheel) walks this exact pair in far more depth; here they simply share the seat every theme's Sunday shares.

cosmos.title: The Week's Duality
cosmos.base: [[Sun and Black Hole]] Sunday's two faces are one star's whole life, compressed: the living Sun burning steady, and the Black Hole every star massive enough eventually becomes when its own light finally runs out — the Ruler's brightest hour and the Servant's own final silence, on the same seat.

continents.title: The Two Poles
continents.base:
[[The Axis]] Sunday's throne is the axis itself — the two poles, held as one dual body the way every theme holds its Ruler and its Servant. They are twins that are opposites: Antarctica a true continent of rock beneath its ice, the Arctic only an ocean frozen over, land and the mirror of land.

[[Eternal Antiphase]] And they keep the dial's own law without being told to — polar day on one answered by polar night on the other, the Ruler's solar noon and the Servant's solar midnight written six months deep across the planet. Reality and its reflection, taking turns with the light.

age_of_heroes.title: The Week's Duality
age_of_heroes.base: [[Lion and Hound]] Sunday's two faces are one family. The Nemean Lion and Cerberus are both children of Typhon and Echidna, which makes this the only dual in the book where the bright face and the dark one are brothers. The Lion is the first of Heracles' labours and the hide he wore afterwards — authority proven and then carried. Cerberus is the twelfth, taken without a weapon, by permission, and given back — authority borrowed and then returned. Ruler and Servant here are not good against evil but one house holding two offices: the crown that is worn, and the door that is kept.

celestial_court.title: The Week's Duality
celestial_court.base: [[The Sage and His Double]] Sunday's two faces are the same face. Sun Wukong takes the title Great Sage Equal to Heaven for himself; the Six-Eared Macaque takes it from him by being indistinguishable — same fur, same crown, same staff, same memories, same conviction. Heaven's mirror fails, Guanyin's incantation fails, and the underworld's register of every soul alive fails, because there is nothing observable to find. Only the Buddha separates them, and what he separates is not a property but a history. That is the whole content of this dual: Ruler and Servant here are not good against evil but an earned title against an identical taken one, and the instrument that can tell them apart does not sit anywhere on the week.

corporate.title: The Week's Duality
corporate.base: [[The Chair and the Board]] Sunday's two faces are two offices of one authority, and this is the only dual in the book that a legal code wrote down on its own. The chief executive runs the company; the board's chairman runs the body that appoints and removes the chief executive. Most modern governance codes recommend the two be held by different people, and the reason they give is exactly the canon's: an authority that answers to nothing is not stronger, only unaccountable. The Ruler's failure is Pride, a delegated power taken as owned. The Servant's failure is Servility, a board that ratifies what it was assembled to govern. Each is the other's only cure.

wow_alliance.title: The Week's Duality
wow_alliance.base:
[[Two Crowns]] Sunday's two faces are both kings, which is what makes this dual an argument rather than a moral. Varian Wrynn holds the bright face: a crown taken from him as a child, a name lost in the fighting pits, and an authority that had to be rebuilt from the lowest position the setting has. Genn Greymane holds the dark one: a crown never lost and a kingdom lost instead, because the wall he built to keep the world out kept the Alliance out with it.

[[What Each Cures]] The Ruler's failure is Pride — the refusal to concede, which is exactly the reflex that survival in a pit rewards. The Servant's failure is Servility, the danger of a king with no kingdom who makes himself the instrument of somebody else's crown. Each is the other's only medicine: Varian is the argument that authority is earned below before it is exercised above, and Genn is the argument that a throne which answers to nothing is not stronger, only alone.

wow_horde.title: The Week's Duality
wow_horde.base:
[[The Appointment]] Sunday's two faces are a Warchief and the successor he named, which makes this dual unlike any other in the book: the shadow was not opposed to the throne, it was issued by it. Thrall built a nation out of a scattered, demon-broken people and then handed it to Grommash Hellscream's son on the strength of a name and a hope. Garrosh razed Theramore, fought a war on two fronts, and had to be removed from the capital by the Horde itself.

[[What Each Cures]] The Ruler's failure is Pride, and Thrall's is precise rather than general: the belief that he could see far enough ahead to appoint the future. The Servant's failure is Servility, and Garrosh's is the version nobody expects — the obedience of a son to a legend, ruling in the outline of a father he never knew and requiring a nation to serve the same outline. Each is the other's only medicine. A throne that cannot admit a mistake produces the successor it deserves, and a successor with nothing of his own to rule by produces the throne he was warned about.

wow_evil.title: The Week's Duality
wow_evil.base:
[[The Same Bargain, Twice]] Sunday's two faces made one decision between them and were answered in opposite ways. Arthas Menethil took a cursed blade in order to save a kingdom that was already lost, and the instrument kept every promise it made. Illidan Stormrage took Sargeras's gift in order to fight the Legion, and the instrument kept its promises too. One was made a king of the dead; the other was buried under a mountain by his own twin for ten thousand years.

[[What Each Cures]] The Ruler's failure is Pride — not vanity, but the conviction that no one else could be trusted with the necessary thing, which is what took Arthas to Northrend with an army he intended to abandon there. The Servant's failure is Servility: Illidan accepted a weapon, then orders, then a summons, and insisted at every stage that the sequence was his own will. Each is the other's only medicine. Pride is corrected by admitting somebody else could have carried it, and servility by admitting nobody made you take it.

cp_gangs.title: The Week's Duality
cp_gangs.base:
[[Two Towers]] Sunday's two faces are both corporations, which is what makes this dual an argument rather than a moral. Arasaka holds the bright face: the oldest continuous power in the setting, a security house that grew into a bank and then into something no state can audit. Militech holds the dark one: an arms manufacturer of comparable size whose entire position runs through a government, and which has therefore never had to answer for itself alone.

[[What Each Cures]] The Ruler's failure is Pride — an order supplied by one party and appealable to nobody, which rebuilt its own tower taller on the ground where it was destroyed. The Servant's failure is Servility, the arms house whose largest customer is also its only regulator and whose executives keep reappearing on the customer's side of the table. Each is the other's only medicine: Arasaka is the argument that an authority answering to nothing is not stronger, only alone, and Militech is the argument that an authority answering to exactly one thing is not safer, only quieter.

cp_street.title: The Week's Duality
cp_street.base:
[[Two Legends]] Sunday's two faces both belong to the same generation and the same bar, which is what makes this dual an argument rather than a moral. Johnny Silverhand holds the bright face: the one figure in the setting who attacked a structure instead of a person, and who has been a political argument ever since precisely because he did not survive to complicate it. Rogue Amendiares holds the dark one: she was offered the same job, refused it, and spent the next fifty years running the room where everybody else's jobs get assigned.

[[What Each Cures]] The Ruler's failure is Pride — a refusal to concede that is indistinguishable from his virtue until the point where everybody who followed him is dead. The Servant's failure is Servility, the fixer's slow conversion of other people's risk into a price list. Each is the other's only medicine: Johnny is the argument that an arrangement everyone has accepted is not therefore correct, and Rogue is the argument that a man who cannot be argued with is not thereby right, only louder.

cp_corpo.title: The Week's Duality
cp_corpo.base:
[[Father and Son]] Sunday's two faces are the same office held twice in one family, which is what makes this dual an argument rather than a moral. Saburo Arasaka holds the bright face: a founder who ran one house for over a century, applied its rules without exception including to his own children, and made an arrangement against the only limit that applies to everybody. Yorinobu holds the dark one: an heir who said in public for years that the house should not exist, killed the man who was it, and then sat down in the chair.

[[What Each Cures]] The Ruler's failure is Pride, and it is metaphysical rather than boastful — a refusal of the end that this cast's own title names. The Servant's failure is Servility: a rebellion that ends in occupying the seat it rebelled against has not escaped the office, it has proved the office stronger than the man. Each is the other's only medicine. The father is the argument that an institution outlives whoever runs it, and the son is the argument that this is not a comfort.

[[The Second Pair]] The dual rotates in lockstep with the Throne and the Ninth. On the alternate turn the same two offices are held by Rosalind Myers, a president who came out of the arms industry, and Colonel Kurt Hansen, who deserted an army and built a state out of the pieces — the identical argument conducted with no surname to inherit.

sw_jedi.title: The Week's Duality
sw_jedi.base:
[[Father and Son]] Sunday's two faces are one office held twice inside a single family, which is what makes this dual the instrument's plainest. Luke Skywalker holds the bright face: no rank, no completed training, and the one decision in the saga that wins by declining to strike. Vader holds the dark one: the same seat's earlier occupant, a man of the largest capability in the cast whose entire adult record is the execution of another man's orders.

[[What Each Cures]] The Ruler's failure is Pride, and here it is conviction rather than boasting — an untested certainty that abandons a training halfway through on the strength of a feeling and walks into a trap built for precisely that. The Servant's failure is Servility, and the indictment is that the service was chosen: he takes the bargain to prevent one loss and becomes the instrument of every loss after it. Each is the other's only medicine. The son is the argument that a person is not finished until the last available act; the father is the argument that the last available act may arrive twenty years late and still count.

[[Why It Is One Seat]] The canon's law for this seat is that opposition is not evil — the shadow face governs, it does not tempt. In this cast the law is literal, because the two faces are the same person's before and after, and the instrument declines to seat them as hero and villain. They are ruler and servant: the one who decides and the one who carries it out, and the whole story is about which of the two roles a man ends up in.

sw_sith.title: The Week's Duality
sw_sith.base:
[[Master and Apprentice]] Sunday's two faces are the two chairs of one doctrine, which is what makes this dual the clearest in the instrument: the lineage itself declares that the office has exactly two seats and that the lower one is filled in order to be used. Palpatine holds the bright face — every promotion conferred, every power granted, an empire produced out of a republic by its own procedures. Anakin holds the dark one: the most capable individual in the cast, acquired at nine and spent entirely on another man's programme.

[[What Each Cures]] The Ruler's failure is Pride, and his is the literal kind — the identification of a person with an institution, announced rather than implied. The Servant's failure is Servility: capability handed over whole, in exchange for a promise about a loss that the promise itself then causes. Each is the other's only medicine, and the medicine is administered exactly once, at the very end, by the servant.

[[One Office, Two Chairs]] Opposition is not evil on this dial; the shadow face governs, it does not tempt. Here the rule has to be stated carefully, because this is the one cast where the tempting is literally what the bright face does. The distinction the instrument keeps is positional rather than moral: the Ruler decides and the Servant carries out, and the reason the doctrine of two is unstable is that the second chair always contains someone strong enough to want the first.

sw_dyad.title: The Week's Duality
sw_dyad.base:
[[The Bond]] Sunday's two faces are the one dual in this instrument whose source material gives it a name of its own. The films call Rey and Kylo Ren a dyad in the Force — a single power held in two bodies — which is exactly the claim the centre of this dial makes about every Sunday it seats, stated for once by the story rather than by the canon. Rey holds the bright face: no house, no rank, no surname, and a record consisting almost entirely of going back for people. Kylo holds the dark one: every inheritance the story has to give, spent in order, and a master at every stage of the spending.

[[What Each Cures]] The Ruler's failure is Pride, and hers is a refusal rather than a boast — an insistence on belonging to nobody, held hard enough to become a claim of its own. The Servant's failure is Servility: two masters killed and two chairs immediately occupied, by a man whose stated programme is to let the past die. Each is the other's only medicine, and the medicine is administered directly, by hand, in the last hour of the story.

[[Not Related, Still One Seat]] Every other Sunday dual in these three casts is a family or a lineage — father and son, master and apprentice. This one is neither, and it is the instrument's strongest evidence that the seat is an office rather than a bloodline. Two people from opposite ends of the galaxy's oldest argument occupy one throne because the throne is defined by the shape of the relation, not by who is in it.

The Slavic Months.base:
[[The Wheel of Labour]] Long before the Roman month-names spread across Europe, the Slavs kept their own calendar — twelve months named not for gods and emperors but for what the land was DOING: the felling of wood, the flowering linden, the swinging sickle, the falling leaf, the ringing frost. Croatia keeps this old reckoning alive to this day, one of the last corners of Europe to say Lipanj where its neighbours say June. This set gathers the twelve Croatian months as proper names — each with the plain English of what it means — and reads the year the way the Slavs first read it: as a wheel of work and weather.

[[The Richer Siblings]] The names are not Croatia's alone. The same roots run through Czech, Polish and Ukrainian, and their small disagreements are the richest story here — the sickle that cuts in July for Croatia and in August for Poland, the linden that flowers a month later north, the leaf-fall that means October in Zagreb and November in Warsaw. Read across the four tongues, the calendar stops being a grid and becomes a map of the season sweeping slowly northward, the same name sliding one month round the year with the frost.

[[On the Pointer]] The twelve are a Calendar-pointer set: twelve marks, one to each two-hour wedge, seated at the pointer's mid-radius so they clear the Earth and Moon that run the rim — the year's own labours mounted on the year's own wheel, opening (like the Almanac beneath them) on the summer crown where the solstice falls.

[[The Art]] Each month's plate is a future work; until it lands, its mark stands empty and named, the word carrying the month on its own.

Siječanj.base:
[[The Name]] Siječanj comes from sijeći, 'to cut' — the sječa, the felling of timber and firewood in the hard cold when the sap is down and the frozen ground bears a sledge. January's Croatian name is a woodcutter's name.

[[The Labour]] It is the deep of winter, the year's first Gregorian month, the cold at its hardest and the days just beginning, barely, to lengthen from the solstice already past.

[[The Siblings]] Ukrainian keeps the very same axe: sichen (січень), January too, cut from the same root. The north names the month otherwise — Czech leden from led, 'ice'; Polish styczen, most often read as the month that joins the old year to the new. Two Slavic minds on one January: one sees the woodcutter, one the ice.

[[On the Pointer]] On the Calendar pointer the Slavic Months ride as a twelve-mark set, one to each wedge at the mid-radius; Siječanj takes the January wedge, low on the dial's left, its first day pinned exactly to the 01:00h line where the Almanac year begins its climb.

Veljača.base:
[[The Name]] Veljača is the puzzle of the calendar — its root is argued to this day. Some read it from valjati, 'to roll or turn', the short month that rolls the winter over toward spring; others from an older velji, 'great', the month that at last begins to make the days great again. Croatian lore simply says Veljača does as it pleases, the most fickle month of the year.

[[The Labour]] It is the shortest month, twenty-eight days (twenty-nine in a leap year), the last full month of winter and the most changeable in its weather.

[[The Siblings]] Here the Slavs scatter widest. Polish luty means 'fierce, frosty' — the biting month; Ukrainian lyutyi (лютий) matches it. Czech unor is read from noriti, the ice 'submerging' as the thaw begins. Croatia's turning month, Poland's cruel one, Bohemia's thawing one — one February seen three ways.

[[On the Pointer]] Veljača takes the February wedge, and it alone runs at its own tempo: twenty-eight days must cover the same thirty degrees the longer months do, so its ring-ticks fall a hair faster — the calendar's one irregular wedge made visible.

Ožujak.base:
[[The Name]] Ožujak carries an old proverb inside it: ožujak laže, 'March lies', the deceiving month whose warm mornings turn to snow by afternoon. The name is most often traced to that same root of falsehood; an older reading hears the sun beginning to gild the land. Either way it is the hinge month, half winter and half spring, trusting neither.

[[The Labour]] March holds the spring equinox, when day and night stand equal and the light half of the year takes the lead; the Gregorian third month, the door of spring.

[[The Siblings]] The north turns to trees. Czech brezen is the birch month, from briza; Ukrainian berezen the same birch. Polish marzec, like English March, borrowed the Roman Mars outright. Croatia's liar, Bohemia's birch, Poland's war-god — three names for one uncertain month.

[[On the Pointer]] Ožujak takes the March wedge, climbing the left of the dial toward the spring equinox — which, by the Almanac's own honest mapping, sits a few ticks clockwise of the wedge line, the natural price of anchoring each month's first day to its hour-line.

Travanj.base:
[[The Name]] Travanj is the grass month, from trava — the weeks when the meadows green and the first real growth covers the bare spring ground.

[[The Labour]] April, the fourth Gregorian month, full spring, the world visibly greening day by day.

[[The Siblings]] The Slavs agree on growth but not on which growth. Polish kwiecien and Ukrainian kviten are the flower month, from kvit; Czech duben is the oak month, from dub. And Ukrainian traven, the grass name Croatia gives to April, it gives to MAY — the same word, one month later east.

[[On the Pointer]] Travanj takes the April wedge on the upper left, the year climbing toward its summit; its mark rides the mid-radius so it never crowds the Earth and Moon that run the ring's edge.

Svibanj.base:
[[The Name]] Svibanj is named for the svib, the dogwood, the shrub whose blossom and reddening wood mark the height of spring — one of the few month-names in Europe drawn from a single wild plant.

[[The Labour]] May, the fifth Gregorian month, spring at its fullest, the last month before summer.

[[The Siblings]] Here Croatia stands almost alone with its dogwood. Ukrainian traven calls May the grass month (Croatia's April name); Czech kveten names it for flowers, and Polish maj borrows the Roman Maia. Croatia's small red shrub against the whole field's grass and bloom.

[[On the Pointer]] Svibanj takes the May wedge, the last before the top of the wheel — for the Almanac opens on June at the very crown, so May closes the ring just short of the summit, spring handing the dial's high seat to summer.

Lipanj.base:
[[The Name]] Lipanj is the linden month, from lipa, the lime tree whose sweet blossom scents the Slavic summer and whose flowers make the tea of every grandmother's cupboard. The linden is the Slavs' own sacred tree, and June is its hour.

[[The Labour]] June holds the summer solstice, the year's longest day and the top of this dial's own year wheel; the sixth Gregorian month, the door of summer.

[[The Siblings]] The linden travels — but not to June. Polish lipiec and Ukrainian lypen are the linden month too, but they name JULY: the same blossom, counted a month later in the cooler north. Croatia's Lipanj and the northern lipiec are the clearest proof that these names follow the FLOWERING, not the calendar.

[[On the Pointer]] Lipanj takes the crown of the wheel, the top wedge, June seated at the dial's summit where the solstice falls — the one month the Calendar pointer opens upon, the linden at the high noon of the year.

Srpanj.base:
[[The Name]] Srpanj is the sickle month, from srp — the curved blade of the wheat harvest, the hottest weeks when the grain is cut. Its name is a tool held in the hand.

[[The Labour]] July, the seventh Gregorian month, high summer, the reaping season across the Slavic plains.

[[The Siblings]] The sickle, like the linden, cuts a month later in the north: Polish sierpien and Czech srpen are the sickle month too, but they name AUGUST. So Croatia's Srpanj (July, sickle) sits where Poland's lipiec (July, linden) sits — the reaping and the linden trading places across the map, one month's drift the whole way.

[[On the Pointer]] Srpanj takes the July wedge just clockwise of the top, high on the dial's right, the year at its brightest and beginning, by a hair, its long decline.

Kolovoz.base:
[[The Name]] Kolovoz is the loveliest compound in the calendar: kolo, 'wheel', and voz, 'cart' — the month of the driving wagons, when the harvest is hauled from field to barn and the cart-wheels never stop turning. A whole month named for the sound of a loaded wagon.

[[The Labour]] August, the eighth Gregorian month, the harvest home, late summer's heat and the granaries filling.

[[The Siblings]] Where Croatia hears wheels, the north still sees the sickle swinging: Polish sierpien, Czech srpen and Ukrainian serpen all name August for the srp, the reaping blade, a month behind Croatia's own Srpanj. The Croatian wagon carries in August what the northern sickle only then cuts.

[[On the Pointer]] Kolovoz takes the August wedge on the dial's right, the year rolling down from its summer crown — the wheel-and-cart month fittingly seated where the wheel of the year turns hardest downward.

Rujan.base:
[[The Name]] Rujan is another of the calendar's argued names, and both readings suit September. One traces it to the stag's rutting roar, the rjuti of the deer as the mating season opens; the other to rujno, the reddening — the red of turning leaves and of the new wine. The bellowing forest or the reddening vine: the month answers to both.

[[The Labour]] September holds the autumn equinox, day and night equal again as the dark half of the year takes its turn; the ninth Gregorian month, the door of autumn.

[[The Siblings]] The reading splits the Slavs cleanly. Czech zari and rijen carry the shining-and-rutting sense across September and October; Polish wrzesien and Ukrainian veresen name September for wrzos, the heather then in bloom. The deer, the red and the heather — three Slavic Septembers.

[[On the Pointer]] Rujan takes the September wedge on the lower right, the year descending toward the autumn equinox, which the Almanac's honest tick-mapping sets a few days clockwise of the wedge line.

Listopad.base:
[[The Name]] Listopad is the plainest and most beautiful of them all: list, 'leaf', and pad, 'fall' — the leaf-fall, October named for the single thing October does. You can watch the whole month happen in the word.

[[The Labour]] October, the tenth Gregorian month, mid-autumn, the leaves down and the year cooling toward winter.

[[The Siblings]] And here is the calendar's greatest crossing. Polish, Czech and Ukrainian ALL keep listopad — the very same leaf-fall word — but every one of them means NOVEMBER by it. Croatia's leaves fall in October; the colder north's fall a month later, and the identical name slides one wedge round the year with them. No name shows the drift more sharply.

[[On the Pointer]] Listopad takes the October wedge at the dial's lower right — and stands as the pointer's own lesson that a Slavic month is a season, not a square on a grid: the same mark reads October here and November a few hundred miles north.

Studeni.base:
[[The Name]] Studeni is the cold month, from studen, 'cold' or 'frost' — November named for the first hard chill, the year's warmth finally spent.

[[The Labour]] November, the eleventh Gregorian month, late autumn tipping into winter, the bare months beginning.

[[The Siblings]] The north, having spent 'leaf-fall' on this month, names it so outright: Polish listopad, Czech listopad and Ukrainian listopad all land their leaf-fall here — Croatia's October name become the neighbours' November. Croatia's cold and the north's falling leaf meet on the very same month.

[[On the Pointer]] Studeni takes the November wedge low on the dial, the year deep in its descent toward the winter solstice and the bottom of the wheel.

Prosinac.base:
[[The Name]] Prosinac closes the year on another riddle. The favoured reading hears prosinuti, the sun 'shining through' — for after the winter solstice the days begin, minutely, to lengthen again, the light breaking back through the dark. An older folk reading remembers the lean midwinter and its begging, prositi. Light returning or the year's hard asking: December holds both.

[[The Labour]] December carries the winter solstice, the year's longest night and the bottom of this dial's year wheel — and, past it, the first turning back toward the light; the twelfth Gregorian month, the year's close.

[[The Siblings]] Here Croatia and Bohemia clasp hands: Czech prosinec is December too, the same shining-through. Polish grudzien and Ukrainian gruden name it for gruda, the frozen clods of earth ringing hard underfoot. The light breaking through, and the ground frozen solid — the two truths of the solstice month.

[[On the Pointer]] Prosinac takes the December wedge at the foot of the dial, the year's midnight — the last of the twelve marks, seated where the wheel bottoms out and, by the same solstice law the whole instrument turns on, begins again.

Sol.base:
[[The Reckoning]] Twelve Gregorian months keep their old shape but carry a flaw no reform ever fixed: 365 days is no whole number of seven-day weeks, so every month's first day wanders the calendar year on year. Moses Cotsworth, a statistician for England's North Eastern Railway maddened by earnings columns that never lined up month to month, proposed the cure in the early 1900s: THIRTEEN months of exactly four weeks each (13 x 28 = 364), every date pinned forever to the same weekday, plus one single day kept OUTSIDE the week entirely to close the year. He named the new month Sol, set between June and July, because it is the one month that carries the summer solstice on its own back.

[[The Day Outside Days]] Year Day falls after the 28th of December and before New Year returns; it belongs to no week, no month, no weekday at all — a single day the reckoning simply does not count. Folded into this dial's own canon: a day kept by no ledger, spent on nothing but itself — the year's one true rest, a day for God.

[[The Company That Believed It]] The reform never won the world, but it won one company outright: George Eastman put Kodak's whole internal accounting on Cotsworth's thirteen months in 1928, and Kodak kept counting that way for sixty-one years — until 1989, long after the League of Nations had already let the idea die everywhere else.

[[The Duality]] Sol is the SUN's thirteenth, and it keeps the year's TOP — the same solstice-crowned wedge June already opens on this dial's own Calendar pointer. Its answer waits at the wheel's foot: Modrenik, the MOON's thirteenth, born in the same blue-moon years, in the year's longest nights.

[[At the Center]] Sol never rides the wheel itself — the Blue Moon Law holds every twelve-set at twelve, always. What a blue-moon year grants instead is rarer: for four weeks around the solstice it already carries — the same twenty-eight days its own name once measured a month by — Sol takes the dial's CENTER outright, the seat an ordinary day gives to its own ruler.

Modrenik.base:
[[The Name]] Modar is the old Slavic word for blue — not the plain plavo of a daylight sky, but the deep bruised blue of dusk, frost and cold iron, the same root Serbian and Croatian still keep for a bruise (modrica). Mesec carries a double meaning no single English word survives: it names the MONTH and the MOON with the same breath, the sky's lamp and the reckoning it keeps, at once. Modrenik is built from both halves together — the month that belongs to the blue moon.

[[The Invention]] No manuscript names Modrenik before this dial: it is owner-sealed, coined to answer a real English idiom — a blue moon, the rare thirteenth full moon a year sometimes carries — in a Slavic tongue that never needed the word, since its own months were already the moon's own count. It is named the way the twelve Croatian months already are: for what the sky is doing, not for an emperor.

[[The Longest Nights]] Modrenik keeps no fixed date. It is cut FROM the instant itself, fourteen days either side of the REAL December solstice, so it always falls across the year's longest nights wherever the solstice itself lands that year — honest across centuries, the way a fixed calendar date never could be.

[[The Duality]] Modrenik is the MOON's thirteenth, and it keeps the year's BOTTOM — the December wedge, the wheel's own midnight, directly opposite Sol's crown. The sun's extra month rides the noon of the year; the moon's rides its midnight — the same throne carried to its own foot.

[[At the Center]] Like Sol, Modrenik never rides the wheel — the Blue Moon Law holds every twelve-set at twelve. In a year with thirteen full moons, for twenty-nine days around the solstice — fourteen either side plus the solstice day itself, as long as one whole turn of the Moon it answers to — Modrenik takes the dial's CENTER outright, the moon's one turn at the seat an ordinary day gives to its own ruler.

The Cube.base:
[[Thesis]] Character is a position in a three-dimensional space rather than a point on a line, and this instrument describes it with three axes instead of with a catalogue of types.

[[Argument]] A single scale running from good to evil can rank people but cannot separate two who rank alike for entirely unlike reasons. Three questions separate them: how much a person acts, what his judgment rests on, and how he holds his own worth. Each question is an axis; each axis has two poles; each pole has two readings, the healthy expression and the fall past it — so a direction is a virtue in measure and a fall beyond it, never a virtue opposed to a vice. The axes are not invented for the occasion. They are the hexagram's own three diagonals, and their six poles are the six arm colors this dial has carried from the beginning; the philosophy and the geometry were the same object before either was named. Because three axes span a space, no enumeration of personalities is required: a small set of rules covers every case, exactly as a handful of movement rules defines every game of chess that will ever be played. Three axes span the space; the LINES through it are thirteen, and counting them is what the rest of this section does.

[[Correspondences]] X, Activation: blue against orange, Composure against Vigor, falling to Lethargy and Frenzy. Y, Moral Scope: yellow against purple-gray, Loyalty against Integrity, falling to Tribalism and Legalism. Z, Self-Regard: green against red, Humility against Dignity, falling to Self-Annihilation and Self-Worship. On the dial the three lines are 12h-24h, 16h-04h and 20h-08h; Y is the vertical, yellow the top face and purple-gray the bottom. THE COORDINATE DOCTRINE follows from the space itself: any figure can be written as a triple (x, y, z) rather than labelled, and the same instrument describes any future entity — a profession, a theme, a season — that has a character to describe. The two seasonal arcs of three read the same six colors as a year: yellow to orange to red is the waning arc from the Summer Solstice, purple-gray to blue to green the waxing arc from the Winter.

[[Quote]] "Know thyself" — the inscription at Delphi, reported by Pausanias (Description of Greece X.24.1).

The Thirteen Axes.base:
[[Thesis]] A cube has exactly thirteen axes through its centre, and that arithmetic — not a preference for symmetry — is what fixes how many characters this instrument can name.

[[Argument]] Three axes run through pairs of faces, six through pairs of edges, four through pairs of vertices: thirteen lines, and therefore thirteen antipodal pairs, because every extreme faces its exact opposite through the centre. One of the thirteen is the Sacred Axis, whose two ends leave the human circle; the remaining twelve carry two ends each, which is where the twenty-four human seats come from — the twelve around the One. The triptych 3 / 6 / 4 is read the same way. The three primaries carry the six offices of the Double Trinity, since persons live on the Sacred diagonal and offices on the faces. Six is man's number, and the six edge axes say why: most people are edge-people, ruled by two extremes at once while holding the third axis in measure. The four vertex axes are the statics of which the two four-station crosses are the dynamics — a star and a fall are the two directions along each of them. Seven and six add the same way the week does: the divine seven of faces and diagonals against the human six of edges, on an instrument built to tell weeks. Even the turning obeys the division — the primaries turn in fours, the vertex axes in threes, the edge axes in twos, which is the crosses' own chiasm repeated in the symmetry group. The cube stands in exactly twenty-four ways, as many as the hours, and its rotation group is precisely the permutations of the four vertex diagonals: the hours permute the crosses, and only the centre never moves.

[[Correspondences]] On the Almanac wheel each of the twelve human axes takes one month: the three face axes on the pure-colour arms of June, October and February, the three human vertex axes on the mixed arms of August, December and April, the six edge axes on the six arms between. On the Rose the same twelve are twenty-four rays, and ray k with ray k+12 ends one axis. The first diagonal ever found here was Judas against Lucifer, humility inverted against worth usurped; the thirteen axes are that discovery generalized until it closes.

[[Quote]] "Who hath measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, and meted out heaven with the span, and comprehended the dust of the earth in a measure?" (Isaiah 40:12).

The One.base:
[[Thesis]] The twenty-seventh cell is the one no turn moves: God at the centre, whom this canon is required to describe twice — by what cannot touch him, and by what he contains.

[[Argument]] The negative description comes first because it is the older discipline. No fall reaches the centre: neither Lethargy nor Frenzy, neither Tribalism nor Legalism, neither Self-Annihilation nor Self-Worship. Six negations are his whole outline, and they are exhaustive — there are only six falls in the system. The positive description is owed beside it, because negation alone would leave an emptiness where the doctrine means a fullness: he holds all six healthy powers at once, Composure and Vigor, Loyalty and Integrity, Humility and Dignity. The centre does not lack the six powers; it contains each without being ruled by any. Zero is therefore not absence but government: no single force rules the whole. Geometry countersigns the theology without being asked to. The centre is the unique fixed point of every rotation of the cube, the unmoved mover in coordinates, and on a dial it is the axle the hands turn around — present the way the centre cubelet of a puzzle cube is present, there, unseen, the only piece no turn ever moves. One consequence is stated as doctrine rather than as an omission: the centre takes no exemplar in any register. Every human example is ruled by something, and a seat whose whole content is that nothing rules it cannot be filled by a person without being falsified.

[[Correspondences]] Perfect Integration at the coordinates (0,0,0), the meeting point of all thirteen axes and the middle station of the Sacred Axis. The Almanac wheel's centre slot holds him alone; the Rose's axle holds the whole sacred trio, which is the same axis seen end-on. On the Banknote the name was already there, since the denomination is THE ONE. Archetypal, historical and modern registers all leave this column empty by doctrine.

[[Quote]] "I AM THAT I AM" (Exodus 3:14); "and by him all things consist" (Colossians 1:17).

The Sacred Axis.base:
[[Thesis]] The Trinity completes on the cube's signed main diagonal — all-minus against all-plus with the centre between: Jesus Christ, God the One, the Devil.

[[Argument]] Three structural facts choose this diagonal over the other three. Sign purity: it is the only line whose ends are wholly negative and wholly positive. Temperature: three cold colours face three warm ones, blue with purple-gray and green against orange with yellow and red. And the sealed seasonal arcs already ran that way, the waxing half from the winter solstice against the waning half from the hot one. Three proofs then arrive from inside the canon. Each person's corner is his two sealed office colours plus one borrowed pole of God's own vertical — the Advocate's blue and the Preserver's green borrow the Creator's midnight purple, the hour of the Nativity; the Destroyer's orange and the Prosecutor's red borrow the Judge's noon yellow, the arm of the usurped accusation — and the two crosses already terminate on exactly those borrowed colours. The solstice architecture is the Church's own, Christmas at the winter solstice against the Baptist at the summer one, whose sentence is the solstice formula itself. And the asymmetry is anti-Manichean: one end holds the healthy readings of its three poles, the other the fallen readings of its three, so they are not mirror gods but a summit of health against a pit of falls — corruption, not a rival principle. The radial law then yields five stations rather than three, since the end of a direction is its fall and its measure lies nearer the centre: Paralyzed Purist, Jesus, The One, Charismatic Champion, the Devil. The Advocate and the Prosecutor are deliberately not equidistant from the Judge — the fall stands farther from God than the virtue by construction, and overshooting past Christ produces the Purist rather than a greater saint. Holiness is not extremism. One distinguishing sentence is owed wherever this axis is taught: the symbolic triad of Advocate, Judge and Prosecutor is NOT the doctrinal Holy Trinity of Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and nothing about the Godhead is being claimed by drawing a line through a cube.

[[Correspondences]] Jesus Christ at (−1,−1,−1) — blue, purple-gray and green, the luminous cold trio of Composure, Integrity and Humility; the Devil at (+1,+1,+1) — orange, yellow and red, the fallen warm trio of Frenzy, Tribalism and Self-Worship; The One between them. One line read three ways, never three systems: Character as cold measure against warm excess, Courtroom as Advocate against Prosecutor, Creation as Preserver against Destroyer. The alias is AXIS MUNDI, Eliade's own term for the world-line through the centre. The two ends leave the twenty-four human hours and display at the centre; their cells keep human echoes — the Contemplative Sage falling to the Paralyzed Purist, the Charismatic Champion falling to the Tribal Warlord. Archetypal: the persons themselves. Historical: Maximilian Kolbe, who took a stranger's place in the starvation bunker at Auschwitz in July 1941, against Nero, the first persecutor and the number the Apocalypse was read against. Modern: Aslan against Sauron, whose shadow can only mock and cannot make — the same privation told as a story. The centre takes no figure.

[[Quote]] "He must increase, but I must decrease" (John 3:30); against "the accuser of our brethren is cast down, which accused them before our God day and night" (Revelation 12:10).

The Sixty-Five Terms.base:
[[Thesis]] This canon names sixty-five things and computes everything else: thirteen axis names, twenty-six luminous readings and twenty-six falls, with every mixed reading left as a combination of named terms rather than given a word of its own.

[[Argument]] The radial law makes each axis five-state — a fall, a measure, the centre, the opposite measure, the opposite fall — so the full character space is the five-cube, a hundred and twenty-five readings spread over twenty-seven geometric seats, counted as one centre, six poles with two readings each, twelve edges with four and eight vertices with eight. Naming all of them would be the enumeration this project forbids: the remaining seventy-two mixed readings are coordinates for describing a real person, computed from terms that already exist, and a person described as measured on one axis and fallen on another needs no new vocabulary to be described exactly. What the naming does buy is a strict triple that every article must satisfy — the SEAT, which is where on the cube; the READING, which says which components are healthy and which have gone past measure; and the EXEMPLAR, the figure who represents that reading. Three laws govern the words themselves. Found names only: every term is lifted from the moral tradition rather than manufactured, which is the FAME FIRST rule applied to vocabulary instead of to people. Different roots within a pair: a cell's luminous and fallen names never share a root, so the pair reads as two things rather than as one thing with a suffix — Composure against Lethargy, never Zeal against Zealotry. And the family-echo law: a compound cell may echo the name-family of a cell it contains, never of a stranger, which is why Tribalism may sound in the Tribal Warlord and Zealotry in the Puritanical Zealot.

[[Correspondences]] Thirteen axis names, twenty-six extremities in two readings each. Alternates stay on record for a deeper pass — Discernment beside Prudence, Contemplation beside Meekness, Entitlement beside Disdain, Service beside Diligence. So does the rejected list, so that no later round re-imports it: crowd phenomena and single acts are not dispositions, a craft is not a trait, and one word was refused for colliding with the Passion of Christ in a canon this biblical. Machiavellianism is deliberately not a grid term — the grid seals no personal names — and survives as the article-level alias of Machination.

[[Quote]] "And whatsoever Adam called every living creature, that was the name thereof" (Genesis 2:19).

The Three Sets.base:
[[Thesis]] Every seat in the Cube is filled three times — archetypal, historical and modern — because a claim about character must survive being made in three different centuries.

[[Argument]] The archetypal set is primary: biblical, mythological and classical-literary figures are the material the vocabulary of virtue was built from, and a seat that cannot be filled from it is probably not a seat but a mood. The historical set is the control — real persons whose documented lives can contradict the seating, which is what makes the seating falsifiable at all. The modern set is the test of currency: if a direction of character cannot be recognized in a story told this century, the reading has become an antique. A figure may appear in more than one place when each face is argued — the color-fidelity law permits many faces, never random ones — which is why Judas holds blue as his night and green as his fall, and the Devil red as Prosecutor and orange as Destroyer.

[[Correspondences]] Twelve figures per set on the six poles, sixteen per set on the eight vertices: eighty-four in all. The three sets are also a reading of TIME on the Rose of the Twenty-Four, where they ride three offset stars — Historical on the star behind the hour, Modern on the star standing on the true hours, Archetypal on the visible star whose rays touch 1h and 13h, because the myths hold in the future too.

[[Quote]] "The thing that hath been, it is that which shall be; and that which is done is that which shall be done" (Ecclesiastes 1:9).

The Activation Axis.base:
[[Thesis]] The X axis asks how much a person acts, and answers with two virtues rather than with a quantity.

[[Argument]] Action is not a scale from idleness to industry with a good end and a bad one. Blue is Composure: the capacity to refrain when acting would be the easier relief. Orange is Vigor: the capacity to spend oneself on a thing that will not move otherwise. Each becomes its own fall by continuing rather than by reversing. Composure held past the moment of need is Lethargy — and this dial names that shadow with unusual precision, since the fall of the watchful color is the failure to keep watch. Vigor spent past its object is Frenzy, motion without a head. The axis is also the one the Character wheel deliberately omits: a flat dial can show two dimensions and only imply the third, and how much a person actually acts is the dimension that life alone reveals.

[[Correspondences]] Blue holds Composure and Lethargy — Siddhartha Gautama, Marcus Aurelius and Yoda against Ilya Ilyich Oblomov, Louis XVI and Jabba the Hutt. Orange holds Vigor and Frenzy — Heracles, Theodore Roosevelt and Conan the Barbarian against Achilles, Adolf Hitler and the Hulk. On the Banknote the axis is N against S, the Nazarene against Sigma: the stilled storm against the mustered host of the Lord of Sabaoth. On the dial it is the 16h-04h diagonal, the Devil's Destroyer seat against Jesus' Advocate seat in the Double Trinity.

[[Quote]] "What, could ye not watch with me one hour?" (Matthew 26:40).

Composure.base:
[[Thesis]] Composure is the negative pole of the Activation axis: the capacity to hold still when stillness is the harder of the two options.

[[Argument]] The virtue is not slowness but governed motion — the accepted cup, the stilled storm, the lamb that opened not his mouth. Its measure is the moment of need: composure that outlasts that moment stops being restraint and becomes Lethargy, the fall in which nothing is refused because nothing is attempted. Oblomov keeps this seat against more famous candidates because Oblomovism is literally the name of the condition the blue fall describes; Hamlet, the better known paralytic, is exact somewhere else — the Paralyzed Purist vertex, where his stillness is a purity problem and not a vitality one.

[[Correspondences]] Blue, the 04h arm — Jesus' Advocate seat in the Double Trinity, the Triads' arm of the past, the Path of Darkness' station of Hate and the Scale's own midnight window. Archetypal: Siddhartha Gautama against Ilya Ilyich Oblomov. Historical: Marcus Aurelius against Louis XVI. Modern: Yoda against Jabba the Hutt. On the Banknote it is N, the Nazarene, whose shadow is the sleeping watch.

[[Quote]] "Peace, be still" (Mark 4:39); "he was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth" (Isaiah 53:7).

Vigor.base:
[[Thesis]] Vigor is the positive pole of the Activation axis: force spent on what will not move without it.

[[Argument]] The virtue is the willingness to be the cause — the labor that clears a road, the deed that ends a delay — and it is a virtue because most things that need doing have no other advocate. Its measure is its object: vigor addressed to a task is strength, vigor that outlives the task is Frenzy, force with no head, which is why Achilles rather than any villain holds the archetypal fall. The same reading seats the Devil twice in the Double Trinity — his orange face is not malice but the office of unmaking, and it is legitimate precisely while it waits for a verdict.

[[Correspondences]] Orange, the 16h arm — the Devil's Destroyer seat, the Prism's arm of Zeal and Courage, and the Path of Light's station of Love, since love as deed is the same force turned toward another. Archetypal: Heracles against Achilles. Historical: Theodore Roosevelt against Adolf Hitler. Modern: Conan the Barbarian against the Hulk. On the Banknote it is S, Sigma the sum, the mustered host.

[[Quote]] "The Lord of Sabaoth" (Romans 9:29); and the shadow's own name, "My name is Legion: for we are many" (Mark 5:9).

The Moral Scope Axis.base:
[[Thesis]] The Y axis asks what a person's judgment rests on: the bonds he holds or the principles he holds.

[[Argument]] Every verdict a person passes is grounded somewhere, and there are only two grounds available. Yellow is Loyalty: the covenant kept, judgment that answers to those it binds. Purple-gray is Integrity: the principle kept, judgment that answers to a rule no party owns. Neither is the other's vice — a world judged only by bonds has no law, a world judged only by law has no mercy — and each falls by being carried past its measure. Loyalty closed to outsiders is Tribalism: one rule for us, another for them. Integrity carried past the reason it was written for is Legalism, the only fall on the Cube that can be committed without a single vice. Its structural reading is Universalism against Particularism, purple first: the pole that answers to a principle no party owns against the pole that answers to its own. This is the axis the Character wheel makes its vertical, because it is the question a compass of character has to ask first.

[[Correspondences]] Yellow holds Loyalty and Tribalism — Penelope, Ernest Shackleton and Samwise Gamgee against David, Pope Alexander VI and Bellatrix Lestrange. Purple-gray holds Integrity and Legalism — Abraham, Socrates and Batman against Inspector Javert, Maximilien Robespierre and Judge Dredd. On the Banknote the axis is G against Omega, the God of the covenant against the letter of the end. On the dial it is the vertical 12h-24h, the one diameter God holds alone in the Double Trinity: Judge at noon, Creator at midnight. The purple-gray of this pole is never royal — it is the moon-gray violet of midnight, the Moon and the Winter Solstice.

[[Quote]] "One jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law" (Matthew 5:18); "the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life" (2 Corinthians 3:6).

Integrity.base:
[[Thesis]] Integrity is the negative pole of the Moral Scope axis: the principle taken as the ground of judgment, at a cost the judge pays himself.

[[Argument]] Its test is not consistency but expense — anyone can keep a rule that costs nothing, and the seat belongs to those who accepted the bill rather than write an exception. Abraham holds the archetypal seat because the demand made on him is the extreme case of a principle against a bond; Socrates holds the historical because he declined the escape that was arranged for him. The fall is the same direction walked past its purpose: Legalism keeps the letter after the letter has consumed its reason, and it is the only fall in the system that requires no vice at all — Javert commits none and dies of one anyway.

[[Correspondences]] Purple-gray, the 24h arm — midnight, God's Creator seat, the Path of Darkness' station of Anger and the Path of Light's Salvation, the Ages wheel's white Death. The hue is moon-gray violet, never royal. Archetypal: Abraham against Inspector Javert (Joseph son of Jacob is the recorded alternate). Historical: Socrates against Maximilien Robespierre. Modern: Batman against Judge Dredd. On the Banknote it is Omega, the letter of the end.

[[Quote]] "He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not" (Psalm 15:4); "the sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath" (Mark 2:27).

Loyalty.base:
[[Thesis]] Loyalty is the positive pole of the Moral Scope axis: the bond taken as the ground of judgment.

[[Argument]] Every verdict rests on something, and the oldest ground anyone has had is a covenant — a promise that binds the judge to the judged. The virtue is measured in years rather than in gestures, which is why its figures are all people who did not leave: Penelope over twenty of them, Shackleton over an ice floe, Samwise up a mountain. Its fall is not the breaking of the covenant but its closure: Tribalism keeps the promise perfectly and denies that anyone outside it has standing, one law for us and another for them. David holds the archetypal fall for exactly this reason — a loyalty to his own house that survives his own justice.

[[Correspondences]] Yellow, the 12h arm — noon, the Judge's own color, the Prism's arm of Joy, the Path of Light's station of Faith. Archetypal: Penelope against David (Ruth is the recorded alternate). Historical: Ernest Shackleton against Pope Alexander VI. Modern: Samwise Gamgee against Bellatrix Lestrange. On the Banknote it is G, the God of the covenant.

[[Quote]] "I will be your God, and ye shall be my people" (Jeremiah 7:23); and the fall's own question, "If ye love them which love you, what thank have ye?" (Luke 6:32).

The Self-Regard Axis.base:
[[Thesis]] The Z axis asks how a person holds his own worth, and both of its healthy answers are accurate rather than modest.

[[Argument]] Green is Humility and red is Dignity, and neither is a quantity of self-esteem: both are estimates, and the virtue in each direction is that the estimate is correct. Humility is worth held downward by someone whose power is larger than his claim on it; Dignity is worth held upright by someone who wears an office rather than owning it. Their falls are the same directions continued until the estimate stops being true. Humility past its measure is Self-Annihilation, the conclusion that one's worth is zero; Dignity past its measure is Self-Worship, the confusion of the office with the man. This axis is the oldest reading on the dial: the Scale of self, whose zero no individual reaches, was drawn here long before the Cube named its coordinates.

[[Correspondences]] Green holds Humility and Self-Annihilation — Jesus Christ, Mahatma Gandhi and Superman against Judas Iscariot, Franz Kafka and Darth Vader. Red holds Dignity and Self-Worship — King Arthur, Nelson Mandela and T'Challa against Lucifer, Salvador Dalí and Lord Voldemort. The strongest pole pair in the whole system is Judas against Lucifer, and on the Cube it is at last a true diagonal — the 20h-08h line the Canon already read as Humility against Pride. On the Banknote the axis is A against M, the Angel against the Master.

[[Quote]] "Whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted" (Luke 14:11).

Humility.base:
[[Thesis]] Humility is the negative pole of the Self-Regard axis: worth held downward by someone whose power is larger than his claim on it.

[[Argument]] The virtue is accuracy, not diminishment — a man with nothing to lower is not humble, he is small. Its archetypal figure is the descent chosen on purpose, the exact counterweight to the climb recorded at the other pole, and the dial has read this pair as a single line since long before the Cube gave it a coordinate. The fall continues the same direction until the estimate stops being true: Self-Annihilation is humility inverted, the conclusion that one's worth is zero. Judas holds it as his second color — his night is blue, the kiss in the dark, but his fall is green: the disciple who annihilated himself standing in the shadow of the master who humbled himself.

[[Correspondences]] Green, the 08h arm — Jesus' Preserver seat, the Prism's arm of Renewal, the Path of Light's station of Hope. Archetypal: Jesus Christ against Judas Iscariot. Historical: Mahatma Gandhi against Franz Kafka (Simone Weil is the recorded alternate). Modern: Superman against Darth Vader. On the Banknote it is A, Alpha, the seed that falls into the ground — and its shadow the grain that dies without bringing forth fruit.

[[Quote]] "Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit" (John 12:24).

Dignity.base:
[[Thesis]] Dignity is the positive pole of the Self-Regard axis: worth held upright by someone who wears an office rather than owns it.

[[Argument]] The distinction the seat turns on is between authority borne and authority possessed. Arthur, Mandela and T'Challa are seated because each holds a crown that plainly belongs to something larger than himself; the office survives the man, and he knows it. The fall is the same direction continued until the office and the man are confused, and it is the only fall in the system recorded as a first-person ambition, which is why Lucifer keeps the seat over every later claimant: the strongest pole pair in the Cube is Judas against Lucifer, and here it is a true diagonal at last. Napoleon, the obvious historical candidate, is seated more exactly at the Messianic Tyrant vertex, leaving Dalí the pure pole.

[[Correspondences]] Red, the 20h arm — the Devil's Prosecutor seat, the Prism's arm of Passion, the Triads' arm of the future, the Path of Darkness' station of Fear. Archetypal: King Arthur against Lucifer (Hector is the recorded alternate). Historical: Nelson Mandela against Salvador Dalí. Modern: T'Challa against Lord Voldemort. On the Banknote it is M, the Master.

[[Quote]] "Well done, good and faithful servant... I will make thee ruler over many things" (Matthew 25:21); against "I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God" (Isaiah 14:13).

Reason ↔ Emotion.base:
[[Thesis]] The first edge axis asks which faculty a person answers with when both are available, and it names two virtues rather than a faculty and its defect.

[[Argument]] An edge cell commits two axes and leaves the third at measure, so this line is Activation and Moral Scope taken together while Self-Regard says nothing. Its cold end joins Composure to Integrity: restraint governing a judgment that answers to a rule no party owns — Prudence, the deliberation that will not be hurried into a verdict. Its warm end joins Vigor to Loyalty: force spent on a bond — Ardor, which is not the absence of thought but thought's subordination to a person. Neither end is the other's fall, which is the point of drawing them as one line: a judge who cannot be moved and a lover who cannot be stopped are describing the same axis from its two ends. Each end falls in its own direction rather than into its opposite. Prudence carried past the moment when a decision was owed becomes Indifference — the deliberation kept up until the case decides itself, reason with the care removed. Ardor spent past its object becomes Vendetta, a bond honoured by ruining what injured it, where the wrong has replaced the person as the thing being served. The discriminator between the healthy readings and their falls is the same on both ends and is worth stating once: a direction is a virtue in measure and a fall past it, so the fall is never a change of heading, only a refusal to stop.

[[Correspondences]] Cold end (−1,−1,0): Prudence falling to Indifference — Solomon and Elizabeth I against Pontius Pilate and Adolf Eichmann. Warm end (+1,+1,0): Ardor falling to Vendetta — Romeo and Joan of Arc against Medea and Genghis Khan. On the Rose the two seats face each other at 17h in red and 05h in blue; on the Almanac wheel the axis takes May, the merry month, at 10h. The axis holds Self-Regard at zero, which is why neither end is about a person's own worth: both are about what the judgment is FOR.

[[Quote]] "Be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves" (Matthew 10:16); "The heart has its reasons, which reason knows nothing of" (Pascal, Pensées).

Prudence.base:
[[Thesis]] Prudence is the cold cell of the Reason ↔ Emotion axis: judgment held back until it can be given, by someone who owes it to a rule rather than to a party.

[[Argument]] The seat is the meeting of Composure and Integrity, and the two make one another possible — restraint without a principle is only delay, and a principle without restraint decides before it has heard. Solomon holds the archetypal reading for an act rather than for a reputation: the verdict is suspended and a test is put in its place until the claim discloses itself, which is deliberation used as an instrument of judgment instead of as an escape from it. Elizabeth I rules under her own motto of watching and keeping silent, and settles religion in 1559 without opening an inquiry into what anyone believes — the same faculty applied to a whole realm. The fall keeps the deliberation and drops what it was for. Indifference is Prudence continued past the moment a decision was owed, and its emblem is the tradition's own: a judgment withheld, hands washed, the case left to decide itself. Its historical reading is the harder one and is stated plainly — deportation administered as a timetable is reason with the care removed, the mechanism a trial in 1961 made a byword. The modern fall says the seat's own sentence out loud, that a living body and a dead one contain the same number of particles, and then leaves for Mars.

[[Correspondences]] The cell (−1,−1,0), Composure plus Integrity, on the Reason ↔ Emotion axis, facing Ardor and its fall Vendetta through the centre. On the Rose it takes 17h in red; on the Almanac wheel its axis holds May at 10h. Archetypal: Solomon against Pontius Pilate. Historical: Elizabeth I against Adolf Eichmann. Modern: Spock against Dr. Manhattan. Self-Regard is at measure here: nothing on this seat is a claim about a person's own worth.

[[Quote]] "He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him" (Proverbs 18:13); against "I am innocent of the blood of this just person: see ye to it" (Matthew 27:24).

Ardor.base:
[[Thesis]] Ardor is the warm cell of the Reason ↔ Emotion axis: the whole of a person's force spent on a bond, in the full knowledge of what the bond costs.

[[Argument]] The seat joins Vigor to Loyalty, and it is not the absence of judgment but judgment's subordination to a person. Romeo spends everything on a bond both houses forbid, which is the archetypal shape of the seat — the fire is not blind, it is aimed. Joan of Arc carries Orléans and the march to Reims in 1429 on an attachment to a crown, and the historical reading is exact because the campaign is documented while the attachment is the only thing that explains it. The modern reading needs one second of screen time: a volunteer takes a sister's place before anyone else has moved. The fall is what this force does when the person it served is replaced by the injury done to that person. Vendetta answers a wrong without measure — envoys murdered and a civilisation annihilated in 1219, a whole life organized around a single sentence until the sentence is spent and its owner has nothing left to be. Medea holds the archetypal fall because she destroys what she loves in order to punish, which is the fall's definition rather than an example of it. The measure line on this seat is not intensity: Ardor and Vendetta burn identically, and differ only in whether the object is still a person.

[[Correspondences]] The cell (+1,+1,0), Vigor plus Loyalty, on the Reason ↔ Emotion axis, facing Prudence and its fall Indifference through the centre. On the Rose it takes 05h in blue; on the Almanac wheel its axis holds May at 10h, the month of the merry name. Archetypal: Romeo against Medea. Historical: Joan of Arc against Genghis Khan. Modern: Katniss Everdeen against Inigo Montoya.

[[Quote]] "for love is strong as death; jealousy is cruel as the grave: the coals thereof are coals of fire" (Song of Solomon 8:6); against "Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord" (Romans 12:19).

Pragmatism ↔ Idealism.base:
[[Thesis]] The second edge axis asks whether a person works with the world as it is or against it as it should be — and both answers are virtues before they are anything else.

[[Argument]] The line commits Activation and Moral Scope in the opposite pairing to Reason ↔ Emotion. Its cold end joins Composure to Loyalty: restraint in the service of a bond, which is Steadfastness — the position held without motion, at whatever length of time the holding takes. Its warm end joins Vigor to Integrity: force in the service of a principle, which is Reform — the world moved because a rule says it must be. The axis is therefore not patience against impatience but two different theories of how a wrong ends: one outlasts it, the other overturns it. Their falls are the sharpest pair on the cube.
